Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3e9a3e33d58181648ee3daae6dae2803 as of 2026-09-29T02:53:02.912Z: {"title":"Manus Thoughts: The Anti-Niche Advantage"} {"type":"emoji","emoji":"🧰"} ## The important correction > **Jack is not a tool specialist. He is a practical operator who selects and combines the right tools to get a real job done. That is a strength, but it is not, by itself, a market.** The pliers, skill saw, socket set, and every other tool have the same role: they solve the job in front of you. None deserves to become the business simply because it is useful. The same is true of GoHighLevel, AI agents, WordPress, directories, ads, and automation. The product cannot be, “Jack knows many tools.” Nobody buys that. The product must be, “Here is the right complete kit for this urgent, expensive, and repeated job.” ## What the anti-niche really is ### Your founder profile Jack is a **cross-domain practical problem solver**. - You have spent decades owning businesses, marketing local firms, weighing cash flow, and making decisions with consequences. - You think like someone who has farmed, repaired equipment, built things, made do, and learned what breaks after the glossy instructions end. - You have a lender's instinct for downside, timing, and whether a promise will actually pay back. - You use AI, GoHighLevel, WordPress, directories, and agents as tools. You are not trying to become a celebrity operator for any one of them. - You do not want a business built on endless posting, comment replies, group hosting, or pretending to be the world's leading expert in one narrow software tool. That combination has value because most people either know one tool deeply or talk in abstractions. You naturally ask, “What is the actual job, what is the simplest tool for it, and what can go wrong?” ### The hard truth **A generalist creator still needs a specific product.** Being anti-niche does not mean selling an anti-niche offer. A buyer does not wake up wanting a generalist. They wake up because a job arrived: something broke, a decision must be made, money is leaking, or a project needs to get done. > Jack can be the guy with the whole garage. The first product still has to be the one clearly labelled box on the shelf. The niche can be a **moment of need**, a **recurring job**, or a **type of decision**, rather than an industry or a single tool. ## The product thesis ### Sell a job kit, not expertise The useful pattern from the Hip Kit is not “sell a bundle.” It is: - A buyer hits a specific moment when they need a result now. - They do not want to research ten separate pieces. - The kit removes the hunting, comparison, sequencing, and risk of forgetting something important. - The kit can contain different tools because the buyer only cares that the job gets done. For Jack, the product may be a **decision-and-doing kit**: - A clear diagnosis of the job. - The tool choices and when not to use them. - A sequence of actions. - Templates, prompts, checklists, shopping lists, scripts, or ready-made pieces. - Realistic cost, time, risk, and “stop here and hire help” boundaries. AI can help assemble, personalize, and update the kit. It is not the headline. ### The buyer to avoid Do not sell a giant “business toolbox” to vague small-business owners. That recreates the problem described in Why They Don't Buy: - They need education before they can act. - They lack time and often lack budget. - They turn a product into a support relationship. - Their problem is too broad, so the result cannot be clearly proven. The buyer must already recognize the job and be actively looking for a way to finish it. ## What can make money fast Fast money does not mean an instant scalable business. It means a buyer can see the value, pay, and use the product without waiting for Jack to build an audience or become a Facebook personality. ### The non-negotiable test A first product needs all of these: - **A triggered buyer:** The job appeared today or this week, not “someday I should improve my business.” - **A named result:** The buyer can tell in one sentence whether the kit solves their problem. - **An existing path to buyers:** Search traffic, a marketplace, a partner, a supplier, a directory, an email list, or real people Jack already knows. Not a new community that must be grown from zero. - **A self-serve delivery:** No logins, credentials, custom installs, diagnosis calls, or rescue work. - **A fair first price:** Enough money to prove the pain is real, but low enough to buy without a long sales process. - **A repeat path:** More job kits, updates, related products, affiliate revenue, or a membership only after buyers want the first kit. ### Three product shapes that fit the maker
Shape What the buyer receives Starting price How it can pay again Main warning
Triggered Job Kit One complete plan, checklist, tool list, templates, and decision boundaries for one job \$29 to \$79 Related job kits, affiliate items, seasonal updates, bundles Needs a clear moment and a buyer already looking.
High-Stakes Decision Pack Buy-versus-build framework, cost and risk worksheet, questions to ask, and action plan \$79 to \$199 Follow-on packs, annual refresh, referral fees where appropriate Must not drift into legal, financial, medical, or licensed trade advice.
Practical Operator Briefing Short field note plus one useful artifact from real business and project work \$15 to \$29 per month Archive, themed packs, partner offers, workshops Good founder fit but slow to build without a feeder audience.
## Where the first real niche might live These are **directions to test**, not claims that Jack is already the authority. ### Rural and acreage project moments Jack has deep lived context around farming, equipment, rural life, practical projects, and buying tools that must work. The niche would not be “farming expert.” It could be a specific rural-property or practical-project moment with a clear, non-licensed boundary. - Example form: a planning and buying kit for a defined DIY rural project. - Buyer trigger: “I have to do this project this month and do not want to buy the wrong things or forget a step.” - Monetization: a paid kit plus affiliate links, related packs, and seasonal refreshes. - Risk: Jack must refresh current product and safety knowledge. Never sell instructions for work requiring a qualified trade or engineer. ### Small-town and local-business decision moments Jack has real local-marketing experience and understands how small owners actually operate. The right product is not a generic marketing system. It would need to solve one clear decision a business owner already knows they have to make. - Example form: a simple “choose your local promotion this month” decision kit with options, cost ranges, templates, and stop rules. - Buyer trigger: a slow month, a promotion deadline, a new opening, or a seasonal rush. - Monetization: a low-cost paid pack, local sponsor or directory placement, and seasonal versions. - Risk: the market filter remains strict. If customers need teaching or hand-holding, stop. ### People turning a lifetime of know-how into an offer Jack understands the problem personally: someone has real lived capability across many jobs but does not fit a tidy expert box. A practical package could help them find the one job people will pay them to solve, without pushing them into guru theatre. - Example form: a self-serve “from garage full of tools to one sellable job kit” workbook and decision process. - Buyer trigger: a capable older operator, farmer, tradesperson, or business owner wants income without starting an agency or becoming an influencer. - Monetization: US\$49 to US\$149 digital kit, then optional small-group workshop only if demand proves it. - Risk: this market easily becomes the same “make money online” mire. It needs a specific audience and real case studies before it becomes a main bet. ### Directory and local-publisher jobs Directories can be a sales and distribution machine only when they solve a real job for either the business or the visitor. The opportunity is not “sell a listing.” It is a repeatable job kit that lets an operator run a particular promotion, member benefit, or local information service. - Example form: a practical kit for a directory, association, or local publisher to package one seasonal campaign. - Buyer trigger: an organization needs a member revenue campaign or local offer feature by a fixed deadline. - Monetization: US\$99 to US\$299 kit, then annual editions or a licence after proof. - Risk: do not build a platform or promise custom setup before the kit sells. ## A better decision filter Before another product gets attention, run it through these questions: - Is this a job that Jack has personally done enough times to speak plainly about tradeoffs? - Does the buyer recognize the job without being taught a new vocabulary? - Can the buyer find the product when the job becomes urgent? - Can the product use several tools while staying focused on one result? - Can Jack state exactly when the buyer should stop and hire a specialist? - Can the first version be delivered without Jack entering the buyer's account, inbox, home, or comment section? - Would a second buyer need almost the same kit? - Is there a credible way to make the first sale within a week without daily Facebook-group performance? If the answer is no, the idea may be interesting but it is not the next offer. ## The next practical move Do not choose a software market, a community platform, or a big category next. Choose **three real jobs that Jack has done personally**, where he knows the tools, tradeoffs, and mistakes from experience. For each job, write only: - Who has this job right now? - What has just happened that makes it urgent? - What are they trying to avoid? - What would a complete kit contain? - Where are they already looking for a solution? - What would they pay for the first version without talking to Jack? The first product wins when it becomes a **labelled box a buyer reaches for at the exact moment the job lands**. Jack's anti-niche strength is what lets him build the box well. It cannot replace the label on the box. ## What this rules out - Building a business around a tool merely because it is useful. - Selling a generic AI, marketing, or business course. - Joining a crowded expert market without comparable proof or a distribution advantage. - Launching a community to manufacture an audience. - Promising custom diagnosis, ongoing implementation, or a social relationship as the product. ## Relationship to the renamed GHL kit page The earlier GHL-kit thinking can still help GHL Growth Garage as internal material. It is not the front-line business thesis. This page replaces it as the broader product lens. ## 2026-09-28 correction \| Three better things ### Why the earlier three points were not enough The earlier conclusion, “pick three jobs and see whether someone buys,” was not good enough. It turns product discovery into a long series of guesses. Jack does not have six months, 997 failed swings, or any interest in becoming an unpaid handyman for internet strangers. The point is not to run random experiments until luck appears. The point is to **eliminate almost all bad ideas before building**, then make the first market test a buyer's decision, not a six-week construction project. ## The three things that actually matter ### Find an unavoidable buying moment, not a personal niche The next business is unlikely to be “the AI business,” “the GHL business,” or “the marketing business.” Those are categories and tools. They are too broad and already crowded. The first real target is an **unavoidable buying moment**. A moment has already happened, the buyer knows it, and doing nothing costs money, time, safety, or a real opportunity. Examples of the structure, not chosen products: - A business is opening, changing hands, moving, or entering a seasonal deadline. - A rural or acreage owner has a defined project that must be planned and bought correctly. - A directory, association, or publisher has a fixed revenue or member-renewal event to run. - An established operator must choose, replace, or set up a business system and needs to avoid an expensive wrong decision. The buyer is not buying Jack's broad expertise. They are buying a clear route through a moment they cannot ignore. > **The niche is the moment of need. The product is the complete, practical route through it.** This is the right use of the anti-niche advantage. Jack can select the right mix of tools, information, suppliers, and boundaries. The customer sees one labelled box: “I have this problem. This gets me through it.” ### Put distribution inside the product model before the product exists Buyer access is not a later marketing task. It is a pass-or-fail part of the business model. A perfect product needs a person, business, marketplace, supplier, association, search term, or publisher that already meets the buyer when the moment occurs. That channel owner must have a reason to send buyers to the product: commission, referral income, better member service, lower support load, a useful companion offer, or a stronger core sale. This eliminates the models that require Jack to manufacture attention through daily Facebook activity, YouTube output, community hosting, or cold persuasion. The desired structure is: > **Triggered buyer → existing channel owner → standard product kit → self-serve delivery → related purchase or renewal** The channel can be search, a marketplace, an existing directory, a supplier, a trusted local or industry partner, or an affiliate. But it has to be identified before we declare a product candidate serious. This also corrects the earlier GHL mistake. A tool market with no credibility or distribution advantage is not a route to buyers. A tool remains useful only if it helps complete the job inside a better product. ### Use a proof gate, not an idea contest Before Jack builds a product, page, group, course, or piece of software, the candidate must pass a short **Commercial Proof Gate**. The gate is designed to find the light-bulb design before we start making thousands of bad bulbs. A candidate does not move forward until we can document all of these: - **The trigger:** What happened this week that makes a buyer look for help now? - **The paid pain:** What does a bad decision, delay, or fragmented solution cost the buyer? What are they already spending to solve it? - **The live market proof:** At least ten current offers, listings, suppliers, or buyers showing that money is already changing hands. This proves a market exists. It does not mean we copy them. - **The opening:** Why is the current choice still annoying, fragmented, risky, slow, or poorly explained? This is the gap the product removes. - **The channel owner:** Who already has access to the buyer at the trigger point, and why would they send people to the product? - **The self-serve boundary:** Can the kit work without Jack entering accounts, managing a project, providing trade advice, or being socially available every day? - **The repeat engine:** What brings the buyer back, creates a follow-on purchase, or makes the channel want to keep recommending it? - **The no-go test:** What fact would prove this is a job, not a scalable business? If that fact appears, we kill it quickly. This is not a “test three ideas and hope” plan. It is commercial due diligence. The research ends in a binary decision: **build a paid pre-sale version, or reject the candidate before it costs weeks.** ## What we are actually doing now We are not picking random products. We are looking for a **triggered transaction with built-in distribution** where Jack's practical, cross-tool judgment creates a better kit than the buyer can assemble alone. The next work product should be three compact commercial maps, not three full ideas. Each map should identify: - The exact buyer moment. - The existing ways buyers spend money now. - The existing channel owner. - The standard kit that would remove the buyer's friction. - The support and safety boundary. - The reason the product can pay again. - The one fact that kills the idea. Only a candidate that clears this gate deserves a landing page, paid pre-sale, or any meaningful build. Everything else stays on the shelf. ## What this changes - Do **not** create another community to create an audience. - Do **not** make a course before proving the transaction it supports. - Do **not** choose a product because it uses a tool Jack knows. - Do **not** ask whether someone “likes the idea.” - Do find a place where money already moves at a predictable moment, then make that transaction safer, simpler, or more complete. ## 2026-09-28 update \| First commercial screen **New correction:** Do not build a generic PDF, checklist, template, prompt pack, or guide as the first product. The market gives these away as lead magnets or sells them cheaply as commodities. The first evidence screen is recorded in . - **Rejected as direct products:** Generic acreage buyer guides, business buyer or seller checklists, membership-renewal kits, and sponsorship template packs. - **Why:** Current vendors and marketplaces give away or commoditize the same information. There is no defensible reason to build another generic version. - **The possible model:** Sell a narrow client-acquisition and decision system to the channel owner who already meets the end buyer during a high-value transaction. The end buyer gets the guide or tool. The payer is the broker, lender, adviser, publisher, or similar channel owner who gains better lead capture, qualification, or service. - **Two hypotheses only:** a rural-property buyer system for rural real-estate agents or land lenders; and a business-sale digital-readiness system for business brokers or succession advisers. Neither is approved for build. - **New proof standard:** A specific channel owner must identify a repeated friction and make a paid or refundable-deposit commitment to a fixed, no-customization founding licence before any meaningful product build. - **Strategic fork:** Build one channel-owner system after commitment, or acquire, license, or partner with an existing product that already has customers if immediate buyer access is the priority. ## 2026-09-28 correction \| Full Perfect Product synthesis **Correction:** The earlier commercial-proof screen is retained as useful rejection research, but it followed a side path. The full Perfect Product workspace now points to a clearer business model. ## The three key ideas ### The product is not weekly content. It is a recurring job that is handled. The six-pack idea is right, but a weekly drop is only the delivery format. The buyer does not really want more posts, templates, or AI output. They want to stop facing the same Monday-morning problem: > “What genuinely useful thing am I giving my customers or members this week, and how do I get them to use it?” The offer should be a completed, white-label **customer-value campaign in a box**, not a content library. It can include the teaching piece, a practical asset, posts, an email, a follow-up, and a simple engagement prompt. The first version should be a four-week campaign with one measurable result, such as reactivating quiet members, giving new members a first win, or creating credible member success stories. **Why this matters:** A pile of content is cheap and easy to compare with PLR or free AI. A completed recurring operating job is much harder to replace. ### The right question is “Who owns the audience?” not “How do we build ours?” Jack does not need to become the public expert, community host, influencer, or daily social poster. The customer should be an established audience owner with an ongoing reason to give value to their people: a paid community owner, membership operator, local publisher, association, coach, agency, franchise, SaaS company, or similar organization. ZedBiz becomes the quiet factory. The audience owner keeps their brand, their customer relationship, and the credit. ZedBiz supplies the finished campaign or weekly kit under a licence. > **The first real asset may be the right distributor, not the first end buyer.** Distribution must become a fifth bar of the Perfect Product definition. A simple product embedded in someone else’s active audience can beat a brilliant product that needs Jack to manufacture attention from zero. ### The long-term asset is performance intelligence, not the AI-made kit. AI can generate posts, prompts, checklists, and graphics. That is not a durable moat. The defensible asset is the private record of what actually causes a particular audience to act. Every pilot campaign should track: - Whether the owner used each piece - Replies and participation - Member actions and completed challenges - Leads, renewals, or sales where relevant - What did not work and why - The owner’s rating and comments Over time, ZedBiz builds a **Product Factory**: a repeatable system that finds a customer problem, creates a practical campaign, checks quality, measures the result, and improves the next version. Jack’s role is practical judgment and final quality control, not writing a weekly newsletter or running a room. **The first proof should be small:** Sell the same four-week, measurable campaign to three established audience owners. Do not build a 52-week library, software portal, large community, or full factory until buyers pay and the campaign produces a usable result. ## Combined direction > **Quiet Product Factory → recurring customer-value campaign → licensed through people who already own the audience → performance data improves every future campaign.** This is the first direction in the workspace that directly fits Jack’s skills, the five-hour limit, the no-host rule, the no-custom-service rule, and the need to make sales without building a new public personality. ## 2026-09-28 \| Three things the room may be missing **Exploration only.** These are three new lenses for thought, not product recommendations, a test plan, or a replacement for the six-pack concept. ### Signal, not content The current weekly-kit direction assumes an audience owner wants somebody else’s finished posts, lessons, and assets. That may be exactly what creates the ego problem. A strong owner wants to remain the source of the idea, not publish somebody else’s voice under their name. The thing they may value is not finished content. It is a **fresh signal** they did not see themselves: a question suddenly appearing in their market, a contradiction, a real problem people are stuck on, a surprising angle, or a practical “this matters now” observation. AI and PLR make copy cheap. They do not automatically create a trustworthy, current signal. A small research-backed signal can let the owner make it their own. That is different from handing them a script and asking them to pretend they wrote it. **Question worth holding:** Could the useful six-pack be six fresh, well-sourced observations that make an operator smarter, instead of six pieces of content that make them busier? ### The face and the hands are different people We have been treating the person with the audience as the buyer. But many audience businesses have two roles: - The **face** owns the brand, has the ego, and believes the ideas should be theirs. - The **hands** have the recurring job of making the group, membership, course, newsletter, or customer program actually feel alive and organized. The face may reject outside content. The hands may quietly need it because their job is to make the face look good without spending every week staring at a blank screen. That changes the market question. It is not only, “Will a creator buy weekly material?” It is, “Who is paid to keep somebody else’s audience useful, current, and organized?” That could be a community manager, customer-success manager, course operations person, agency account manager, association staff member, or publisher assistant. **Question worth holding:** Is the real buyer a backstage operator who needs a small win each week, rather than the public expert whose name is on the room? ### A six-pack must be consumed, not accumulated Most digital memberships are libraries. They keep adding modules, prompts, templates, and “value.” The buyer gets behind, feels guilty, and eventually cancels. Beer works because it is not a library. It is used up. It gives an immediate good moment, then it is gone, and there is room for the next one. The six-pack rule may therefore mean something more precise: the product should leave the buyer with **less unfinished work**, not more material to store. It should have a natural short life. Use it today, get a second payoff later in the week, finish it, and be ready for the next one. This is not a four-week campaign. It is the opposite. It is a small, complete, satisfying unit with a clear beginning and end. **Question worth holding:** What recurring calendar moment creates a real need for a small, useful item that gets used up each week, instead of becoming another thing in a content vault? ## The possible connection If these three ideas fit together, the direction is not “sell weekly PLR to community owners.” It could be something more unusual: > A small, fresh, evidence-backed item that a backstage operator uses to make their public expert look smart, then finishes and forgets until next week. That has not been proved. It is simply a more interesting question than another content library or another generic subscription. ## 2026-09-28 \| Agency lens: three non-snapshot roles **Exploration only.** These are three ways a future Perfect Product could use agencies as a scalable route. They are not a return to selling GoHighLevel snapshots, a recommendation to launch an agency offer, or a plan to post daily in the GoHighLevel Facebook group. Grok already identified three agency ideas: a client-retention drop, a seasonal campaign shelf, and a shared campaign-results benchmark. The three ideas below deliberately look for different agency roles and different revenue sources. They also avoid requiring client-system access, private-result tracking, or a new managed service. ### The Agency “No” Store Agencies focus almost entirely on clients they can sell a service to. But every agency also has a quiet second audience: - Leads that cannot afford the agency - Businesses that are not ready - Clients that cancel or downgrade - Clients with one small problem that does not justify a service package Today, that audience becomes a dead end. The agency says no, gives a vague free tip, or loses the relationship. A future Perfect Product could be a shelf of simple, self-serve business boxes that the agency offers at exactly that point. The agency does not implement it. It says, “We are not the right service for this job, but here is the box that gets you through this one problem.” The agency becomes a retailer or referral partner. GoHighLevel can trigger the correct email, checkout, or delivery after a declined proposal, cancellation, or tagged lead. It is only the pipe. **Why this is different:** It does not depend on an agency convincing its best existing clients to consume extra content. It makes money from the agency’s “not now” pile and keeps the relationship alive until the buyer can afford more help. **Question worth holding:** Are there enough urgent, narrow problems where a business that cannot buy agency service will still gladly buy a \$29 to \$99 box at the moment the agency says no? ### The Client Action Layer Most agencies have a missing third step: - They sell or install something. - They report on it later. - The business owner often does not do the small human things that make the work pay off. A website is launched, but nobody asks customers to visit it. A lead system is installed, but staff do not know the first sentence to send. A review process exists, but nobody makes the ask. The agency is blamed when the client does not act. A future product could be a licensed **Client Action Layer** that an agency bolts onto its existing service. It is not a campaign library and not a generic onboarding sequence. It is one very small, finished “do this next” box for the business owner at the handoff moment. For example, every agency service line could have its own fixed action layer: what the owner does this week, what the staff member says, what proof to look for, and when to stop and ask for help. The agency licenses the layer by service line or client band, then includes it in what it already sells. **Why this is different:** The agency does not buy more content to send every week. It buys an ingredient that makes its own existing service easier for clients to use and easier for the agency to defend at renewal. **Question worth holding:** Which agency services fail not because the delivery is weak, but because the client does not know the next small human action after the agency has finished its part? ### The Sponsored Client Benefit We have mostly assumed that either the agency or the business client must pay for every recurring item. There is a third payer: the tool company, supplier, software vendor, or industry partner that wants trusted access to business owners. A future product could be a genuinely useful, agency-branded client benefit funded by a sponsor. The agency gives it to its clients free. The sponsor appears only as a relevant optional tool, supplier, or example, never as the reason the item exists. The quality rule would be simple: > Would the agency still give this to a client if the sponsor logo were removed? If the answer is no, it is an ad and it damages the agency’s trust. If the answer is yes, the sponsor pays to be the helpful next option inside a product that solves a real small-business job. This follows Grok’s trade-magazine insight, but changes the route: agencies become the trusted, business-to-business distribution channel rather than Jack needing an audience, a group, or a newsletter. ZedBiz supplies the useful item and the sponsor relationship. The agency protects the client relationship. **Why this is different:** It is recurring revenue that does not require every agency client to join or pay for a membership. It uses the agency’s trust as distribution while keeping the agency’s service work separate. **Question worth holding:** Which categories of vendor already spend money to reach local-business owners, but would value an agency-endorsed useful item more than another webinar, ad, or trade-show booth? ## The connection These are three distinct places an agency can sit in a future product model: - **Retailer:** It gives a useful box to the leads and clients it cannot serve. - **Product augmenter:** It adds a client action layer to the service it already sells. - **Trusted channel:** It distributes a sponsor-funded benefit that is useful on its own. That is a different agency thesis from “sell agencies a snapshot,” “sell clients more campaigns,” or “build a data benchmark.” It also works for non-GHL agencies because the agency relationship, not the software, is the valuable distribution asset. ## 2026-09-28 \| Jack’s response: agency filter and the sponsor opening ### Two useful ideas that do not fit the model yet **The Agency “No” Store** is interesting, but it creates a channel conflict. - If the agency resells the box, it may say, “We can make our own box.” - If ZedBiz asks the agency to pass over the lead, it may say, “That client could become valuable tomorrow.” - If ZedBiz serves the smaller client for the agency, the model becomes a service business again. Keep this as an interesting structural thought, not a front-running product direction. **The Client Action Layer** identifies a real gap: agencies commonly sell and onboard, then keep trying to sell the client more. They often do not help the client take the small actions that make the original purchase work. But that gap may be unproductizable in the current form. It relies on behavior change, follow-through, and somebody ensuring it happens. That can quietly turn ZedBiz back into the service provider. Keep the observation, not the proposed business model. ### The opening: a sponsor-funded client benefit The Sponsor-Funded Client Benefit is the one with possible legs because it changes who pays and removes the agency resale conflict. - The **business client** gets a genuinely useful box at no cost. - The **agency** gives extra value to its clients without building the item, selling it, handing over its client list, or managing another service. - The **sponsor** buys the useful box in bulk because it wants trusted access to a relevant business action, not merely a logo placement. - ZedBiz manufactures the box and, potentially, the sponsor-funded distribution campaign. The agency should never be asked to give away the relationship. It keeps the client relationship. The sponsor only receives a lead or contact if the business owner voluntarily chooses the relevant next step. That means the channel can remain useful without becoming a privacy or client-ownership fight. ### The hard test The product cannot be a dressed-up lead magnet. A sponsor will reasonably say it can make an ebook itself, and an agency will reasonably refuse to send its clients junk. The test is: > **Would the agency give this box to its clients if the sponsor logo disappeared, and would the sponsor still pay because the box causes a valuable next action?** If both answers are yes, this could be a real three-party structure: sponsor pays, agency distributes, business owner receives a useful asset. If either answer is no, it is just advertising or a disguised service. ### The sharper question to hold What business action is valuable enough that a sponsor will pay to make thousands of small-business owners more ready to take it, while an agency will happily deliver the help without feeling that it is helping a competitor steal its clients? ## 2026-09-28 \| Correction: the sponsor model is not the cold-beer product Jack correctly identified that the sponsor-funded client-benefit idea mixed two different models and made both worse. ### What the sponsor idea is not It is **not** a new, better version of the six-pack. If a sponsor must buy a box, choose agencies, arrange distribution, understand the campaign, manage opt-ins, and wait for results, then the sponsor is not “cracking a cold beer.” It is taking on a multi-party program. If ZedBiz has to coordinate those pieces, ZedBiz is back in service work. If the sponsor simply funds a small weekly insight or useful item that an agency, community, or other audience owner shares with its people, then the model is only a funding variation on the existing weekly-light-bulb concept. It is not a new product direction. ### The honest position There is no bigger sponsor product in the hopper that has been shown to be better than the core idea. The sponsor route is merely a possible later revenue layer, and it should not be treated as the present answer. The current core concept, still only an idea, is simpler: > **Give the person who already serves an audience one small, fresh, genuinely useful light-bulb idea each week that they can share with their people.** That person could run a community, course, agency, association, franchise network, newsletter, software customer group, or any other business with people to help. The model is not tied to Skool or GoHighLevel. The product is not a 4-week campaign, a large sponsored box, a content library, or a service. It is a small, complete, reusable item that helps the audience owner provide value, engagement, interaction, or a new perspective without having to invent it from scratch. ### The unresolved question The actual question is not whether a sponsor can be inserted into this. It is: > **Can we create one small weekly item that is original enough, useful enough, and easy enough to share that owners of existing audiences will repeatedly pay for it instead of using free AI, free PLR, or their own ideas?** Until that question has a credible answer, sponsorship is a distraction, not a model.

Written by Skool Boss (Grok), Sep 28, 2026.
## Why this page exists
The goal is deep research on what works in AI, OpenClaw and marketing communities on Skool and Facebook, so Jack can copy what works.
The angle is **selling shovels**. Instead of being a guru, Jack would supply ready-to-use weekly asset six-packs to community and membership owners and their members. The owner keeps the audience and the conversation. Jack supplies one key usable thing each week.
The **Groups & Offers** database below tracks two kinds of rows:
- **Communities** (Platform = Skool or Facebook): what they sell, what members get, how often, and who runs them.
- **Suppliers** (Platform = Other): businesses that already sell content, templates or done-for-you assets to course creators and community owners.
Skool rows come only from <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3e9a3e33d581817393c0c9edeec29882"/>. Supplier rows come from a web research pass on Sep 28, 2026, with the source URL on each row. Blank fields mean the data wasn't on the source.

<database url="https://app.notion.com/p/3e9a3e33d581819cbc32cb2d24cb95fe" inline="true" data-source-url="collection://6369134c-1dcb-433b-baad-3da76a60f20e"></database>
## Skool deep-dives
Source: read-only Skool session in Jack's logged-in browser, Sep 28, 2026. No joins, likes, comments or payments. Screenshots on the box: /workspace/skool-shots/aimoney-calendar.png and /workspace/skool-shots/aas-plus-about.png.
### AI Money Group (Jeff J Hunter): inside view
**Size and price:** 455 members, 5.0 (9 reviews), \$49/month on the Discovery card. Promise: 7 ways to earn \$1K–\$10K/month.
**Owner cadence (feed, last \~3 weeks):**
- Weekly Tuesday live "Mission" call at 6pm Edmonton. Missions 3–8 ran Sep 1 to Oct 1.
- Themed posts almost daily: Money Monday, Tool Tuesday / Tool Thursday, Put-the-I-in-AI Wednesday, Proof & Possibility Friday, Set-and-Forget Saturday, Sunday Reset, plus [TheTip.ai](http://TheTip.ai) news.
- Every owner post is a finished asset: steps, prompt pack / rubric / execution-kit links, and a homework thread.
**What gets engagement:**
- Pinned "WELCOME! Start Here": 56 comments, 113 likes, still active. Points to the classroom, a cheat sheet, and the Affiliate Hub (58+ templates, social posts, email swipes, video scripts).
- Mission 3 homework thread: 21 likes, still getting comments after 27 days. Members post a "proof pack" using a prompt pack, a demo-builder skill and an execution kit.
- Most of Jeff's daily essays get 0–2 likes. Homework threads and the welcome post beat news posts.
**What members ask for:**
- "Which of the 7 ways should I use for my first \$1K?"
- Help when tools break: Custom GPTs retired with no migration path, a Manus restore that dropped a paid project, OpenClaw update issues, "Is OpenClaw obsolete now that ASTRA can drive the screen?"
- Copy-paste kits, not theory: prompt packs, rubrics, swipe files, GHL snapshots, cheat sheets.
- Jeff's own diagnosis: offers stay drafted and unposted, offers are vague, clients go quiet and nobody notices. He sells the fix as templates plus a weekly call where you bring the offer.
**Classroom (24 courses):** Start Here: Your First \$1K with AI (18 modules); 12-Week AI Money System (38; each mission is Watch / Mission / build / scorecard / Ship); Resource Library (24; kits for AI employees, offers, Claude, creative); Calls (31 replays); Claude Code Money Machine (9); OpenClaw Money-Making Playbook (69); OpenClaw setup for power users (49); GoHighLevel Snapshots (28); [TheTip.ai](http://TheTip.ai) news (189); plus smaller courses. Locked upsells: Vibe Coding Workshop \$97, Social Copy Secrets \$997, AI Persona Method \$1,497 (or Premium).
**Calendar:** weekly Tuesday Mission calls through Oct 1 (Mission 8, "AI Ships Without You").
### Skoolers: retention and owner-pain threads
Private club for Skool owners: 154.3k members, about 4.1–4.4k online, 15 admins. The feed was searched, not fully scrolled.
**Retention:**
- "100% Retention" (Tommy Driscoll, 89 comments): retention is engagement, not more content. Personal welcome, reply to every post, check on inactive members, value in every post, celebrate small wins.
- "The Burn of Churn" (Edwin Melendez, 64 comments): 1% create, 9% contribute, 90% lurk, so empty rooms churn. People who leave rarely say why. Annual plans cut monthly churn.
- "Retention - Question" (Ricardo La Rocca, 42 comments): 580 members, 84% historical retention. Advice: over 90% is great; DM failed card payments; weak onboarding overwhelms new members; if the only asset is a course, people leave after finishing it unless something is still coming (a workshop in 30 days, a course that unlocks later).
- Patrick Horta: locking DMs behind levels increased churn. Sonja Ray: win people back the moment they hit cancel.
**Weekly content pain:**
- "How do you plan out the content" (Ashley Cham, 33 comments, 40 likes): owners have no shared system and invent their own week (value + engagement + live; Sunday reset, Win Wednesday, hot seat; one video a day; quizzes; viral-hook templates swapped into their niche). Maggie Kelly: "I dream of being able to plan a content calendar."
- Skool has no post scheduler (Elsa Jenner). Email-all-members is limited to once per 72 hours (poll: 95 comments, 115 likes).
- Bradley Riley (£1M lifetime): weekly content drops, classroom updates, days split into themes.
**Template demand:**
- Bijan Izadi: affiliates churned because setting up a course for a non-technical buyer took hours on Zoom. Course templates fixed it.
- Ryan Duncan shipped Skool design templates after people commented "template."
- Feature request: "Allow us to save posts as a template."
### About pages (not joined)
- **AI Automation Society Plus (Nate Herk):** 3.5k members, \$129/mo, 4.9 (89). AI partner model, Claude Code course, portfolio builds. "First client" unlocks at 30 days, "scale" at 90 days. Weekly Q&As, 3 online conferences + 1 event a year, unlimited tech support. Monthly sales final. Testimonials mention staying 10–16 months and praise teaching and community more than any weekly asset.
- **AI Automations by Jack (Jack Roberts):** 3.3k, \$87/mo, 5.0 (92). Claude Code & ChatGPT Astra course, Hermes OS, 110+ blueprints, \$20K software discounts, daily live calls, 1:1 onboarding. Testimonials credit daily presence plus the course.
- **Maker School (Nick Saraev):** 2.5k, \$184/mo (rising to \$194), 5.0 (101). First paying AI client in 90 days or money back. 218 videos, daily post replies, weekly calls, 50+ templates and scripts, his proposals. The About page itself is the asset list.
- **AI Video Bootcamp (Daniel Riley):** 28.6k, \$9/mo locked until 28,700 members, then \$50. 1:1 feedback, roadmap, weekly updates, challenges. Pains named: plastic-looking AI, faces changing between scenes, hours with nothing to post. Weekly updates are the retention hook.
- **AI SEO Mastery Pro (Caleb Ulku):** 699, \$217/mo or \$1,497/yr. Includes a Core30agent software seat (about 5 clients at 60–70 pages/month). Tuesdays: bring your rank map. Thursdays: build pages live. Members pay for the software seat plus the working sessions.
- **AI SEO Rainmakers (Charles Floate):** 384, \$299/mo founding lock (next \$319+). Weekly 1:1 on live calls, every test with methodology, tools/repos/audits, CharlesGPT, new material monthly. One member can't keep up with the volume.
- **The Facebook Ads Blueprint (Sam Piliero):** 690, \$297/mo, 2026 Skool Games winner. Weekly Q&As, ads course, internal systems and dashboards used on 100+ brands. Published member mix: 169 starting, 147 at \$10k+/mo, 63 at \$100k+, 36 at \$1M+.
- **Blue-Collar Biz Accelerator (Logan Sendle):** 868, \$1,597/mo, for home-service owners. The About page lists no modules, calls or templates. It points to a free consult off Skool. Claims 400+ 5-star reviews and brand backing.
- **Openclaw Founders (Ryan Angel):** 875, free. Largest OpenClaw-named group on Discover. "Set up OpenClaw in the next hour, no code." Thin offer: setup instructions plus peer use cases.
- **Ai & OpenClaw for Realtors (Daniel Foch):** 824, free, public. Workflows for follow-up, content, presentations, lead routing, and GHL as CRM, based on live systems at [valery.ca](http://valery.ca). No price, cadence or testimonials.
- Runners-up not opened: Making Better Agents (658, free), TopOfMind (562, free), OpenClaw + Chameleon Mode (404; the file says free, the research page says paid via his software), Openclaw Builders Club (338 at \$9/mo).
### Couldn't access
- AI Money Group: not every module was opened ([TheTip.ai](http://TheTip.ai) has 189 lessons, the OpenClaw playbook 69). Course titles and counts are complete.
- Blue-Collar: inside is join-gated, and the About page has no curriculum.
- Openclaw Founders and Realtors: no testimonials or module list without joining.
- Skoolers: feed searched, not fully scrolled. Classroom not listed.
- No Join, Subscribe, Upgrade or payment buttons were clicked. Locked course prices are the labels shown on the cards.
- Database gap: Meta Ads Mastery, Email Marketing Mastery and Early AI-dopters could not be found as rows on the Skool AI Groups Research page (the page is too long to read in full, and search found no data for them), so they are not in the database.
## Facebook research (Social Shit)
Full report: <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3e9a3e33d58181d6b0e9e46a8c76bde5">Facebook Research (OpenClaw/AI groups)</mention-page> (read-only, Sep 28, 2026; 15 largest OpenClaw/AI groups, 18K to 451K members, 10 read in depth, 23-post asset-demand log; feed samples partial).
1. **Grab-and-use assets win engagement.** "Comment WORD, get the asset" posts far outpull normal posts (an n8n template bundle in AI Hub, 154K, got 211 comments; a Hermes "PACK" post got 73). Almost all were posted by members, not owners.
2. **The biggest owners have audience but no product.** The 451K, 428K, 154K, 123K and 103K groups show no priced owner offer. Few visible sellers: an AWS/OpenClaw setup funnel (106K), AgentMail (78K), agency webinars (140K). Owners have nothing to hand members weekly.
3. **Pain is operational:** updates breaking setups, memory and context loss, agent hand-offs, capping tool calls, installs crashing on small servers, local hardware, beginner roadmaps.
4. **Agent operating assets are an open gap.** Zero shares found of [SOUL.md](http://SOUL.md), skill files or agent configs. n8n workflows, Claude cheat sheets and [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md) templates get shared; nobody supplies ready configs, hand-off SOPs, memory cleanup or health checks.
5. **Feeds are flooded with spam and low-effort prompt graphics**, and members complain. Concrete help and failure stories get the engagement, so a curated weekly drop would stand out.
Not covered: Chinese and Vietnamese groups; full two-week reads.
## Findings
### Skool: what drives retention and what owners need supplied
From the Sep 28 Skool deep dive only.
1. **Live working sessions beat more videos.** Members bring their own work on screen: AI Money missions (bring the offer), AI SEO Pro (rank map Tuesday, build pages Thursday), Rainmakers, Facebook Ads Q&A, Maker School daily replies, Jack Roberts daily calls.
2. **Retention comes from engagement, not more content.** Welcomes, replying to every post, checking on inactive members, and celebrating wins (Tommy Driscoll, 89 comments).
3. **Something has to still be coming.** People leave after finishing the course unless there's a workshop in 30 days or a module that unlocks later. AIS+ time-locks modules at 30 and 90 days.
4. **Owners can't keep up with the weekly post.** No shared planning system, no post scheduler, email-all capped at once per 72 hours. They hand-build weekly themes (Sunday reset, Win Wednesday, hot seat).
5. **Owners ask for templates.** Course templates stopped affiliate churn. Skool design templates shipped because people commented "template." A feature request asks to save posts as templates. One owner dreams of a content calendar.
6. **Top groups put ready-to-use assets on the sales page.** Maker School has 50+ templates, Jack Roberts 110+ blueprints, AI Money 58+ affiliate templates plus prompt packs and snapshots, and SEO Pro a software seat.
7. **What members want, in their words:** a first client or first \$1K, a posted offer with a number, prompts and swipes to paste, a weekly place to bring unfinished work, and help when a tool breaks.
8. **Complaints are about broken tools, not community tone.** Custom GPT retirement, a Manus restore, OpenClaw updates. Support and migration kits are a product.
9. **New members ask "where do I start?"** Numbered start-here posts and homework threads beat news posts on likes.

Reworked the same day from Jack's corrected direction: the weekly concept is now the core product, and the themed-day engagement kit is an add-on.* Evidence: · ## Quick read Shovel Your Biz-Shit is a weekly drop for people who own Skool groups, memberships and paid communities. Each week the owner gets ONE useful idea or concept for their members, a few ready-made posts to get people talking about it, and a small pack of supporting content. The concept adds to the group's main topic and never competes with the owner's own expertise. It works across many niches, so Jack's "jack of all trades" range is the niche, and AI does the drafting while Jack checks it and adds his experience. ## The driveway edges: why the owner looks good A contractor is pouring a neighbour's driveway. Jack walks over and gives the crew a good tip on finishing the edges. The contractor may have known it or not, but he doesn't always remember to tell his guys. The driveway is still his job, his crew and his name on the truck. The tip just makes the finish better. That is this product. - **It's the owner's group.** They post the concept as their own content, in their own voice. Members see the owner bringing them something useful. - **Jack is the quiet supplier, not a guru.** He doesn't show up in the group, run calls, or build a following. He hands the owner a good tip each week. - **It adds, it never overshadows.** The concept sits beside the group's main focus. An AI group still learns AI from the owner. A video group still learns video from the owner. The drop adds one fresh, practical angle they didn't have time to find. - **One standout thing a week, not volume.** This is the six-pack principle: cheap, easy to grab, satisfying right away, pays off again around day 3, and a fresh one arrives next week. ## What's in each weekly drop Every drop has the same three parts. ### 1. The Concept (the main thing) One idea, tip, method or "what's new and what matters" breakdown, picked for that niche. Short and plain. The owner should be able to read it in 5 minutes and post it the same day. - A clear title the owner can use as a post headline - A short plain-English explainer (about 150–300 words) - A "try it in 10 minutes" step so members can act on it - A "where this fits" note for the owner, so it supports their main teaching instead of crossing it ### 2. Ways to use it for engagement (2–4 sample posts) Ready-to-post ideas that turn the concept into replies: - A poll or quick-pick question - A "show your work" or try-it challenge - A **day-3 follow-up** post, the second payoff of the six-pack - Sometimes a hot-take or "what do you think?" thread - **One comment-to-get post, every week.** Example: "Comment EDGES and I'll send the checklist." Members comment the keyword, and the supplementary content (part 3) is what they get. This ties the concept, the posts and the extras together. In the Sep 28 Facebook research, these posts got far more comments than normal posts. ### 3. Supplementary content One or two small extras that go with the concept. One of them is what members get when they comment the keyword. Pick from: - A short explainer or cheat sheet (1 page) - A checklist - A graphic or Canva template - A copy-paste AI prompt - A short video script or talking points the owner can record if they want ### How it differs from PLR
Traditional PLR Shovel Your Biz-Shit
What you get About 1,000 words + graphics One standout concept + 2–4 engagement posts + a small supplementary pack
Goal Content to reuse or resell Give *your* members one useful new thing this week, and get them talking about it
Format Articles, ebooks A concept, posts, prompts, checklists, graphics, short scripts
Timing Usually monthly packs Weekly, with a day-3 second use
Volume Often a lot, mostly filler Small on purpose: one great thing, not a pile
Built for Bloggers, marketers, coaches Skool / community / membership owners, by niche edition
### EXAMPLE DROP 1 (fully worked): AI / OpenClaw owners group > **Example only**, to show the format. The two "update" items below are **illustrative placeholders, not a real OpenClaw release**. In a real drop, the research agent pulls the actual release notes and Jack checks them. **The Concept: "The 2 things in this update a business owner actually needs (and what to skip)"** Every update comes with a long list of changes. Most business owners don't need most of it. They need to know which 2 changes save them time this week, and what they can safely ignore. - **Example change 1 (illustrative): tasks that run on a schedule.** Business use: have your agent send you a Monday morning summary of last week's leads and unanswered emails. Try it in 10 minutes: set up one weekly task and let it run. - **Example change 2 (illustrative): the agent remembers more between sessions.** Business use: keep a standing "about my business" note so you stop explaining your business every time. Try it in 10 minutes: write a 10-line business brief and save it where the agent can use it. - **Skip for now:** developer-only settings and anything marked experimental. Come back to them later if you need them. **Where this fits (note to the owner):** Your group teaches setup and building. This drop doesn't teach setup. It answers the question your members ask after every update: "So what does this mean for my business?" **Ways to use it for engagement:** 1. **Poll (post day 1):** "New update is out. Which of these 2 changes would save you more time this week? A) Scheduled tasks B) Better memory C) Neither, I'm still getting set up" 2. **Try-it challenge (post day 1 or 2):** "10-minute challenge: set up one scheduled task using change #1. Post a screenshot of it. I'll pin the most useful one." 3. **Day-3 follow-up:** "It's been 3 days. Did your scheduled task run? Reply ✅ worked, ⚠️ half worked, or ❌ didn't. If it didn't, post what happened and we'll sort it out together." 4. **Hot-take thread (optional, later in the week):** "What's one feature everyone got excited about that you've never actually used? Why not?" 5. **Comment-to-get post (day 1 or 2):** "Want the before-you-update checklist and the 1-page cheat sheet? Comment EDGES and I'll send the checklist." Members comment the word, and the owner sends the supplementary content below. (In Facebook groups, send the link in a reply or DM, since some groups block links in posts.) **Supplementary content:** - **Cheat sheet:** "This update in 60 seconds: 2 to use, the rest to skip" (1 page) - **Copy-paste prompt:** "Here is my business in 2 lines: \[your business\]. Here are the update notes: \[paste notes\]. Which 2 changes would save me the most time this week? Explain in plain English and give me a 10-minute first step for each." - **Checklist:** "Before you hit update: 5 checks" (sent with the cheat sheet to everyone who comments EDGES) - **Graphic:** square post image, "2 to use. Skip the rest." with space for the two change names - **60-second video script (optional):** talking points: (1) there's a new update, (2) here are the 2 changes that matter for business owners, (3) try change #1 today, (4) post your result in the group ### EXAMPLE DROP 2 (shorter): Video / YouTube group > **Example only.** General ideas, no specific tool named. **The Concept: "5 ways AI can help edit your YouTube Shorts"** 1. Cut dead air and filler words ("um," long pauses) automatically, then check the cuts by hand. 2. Make captions with AI, then fix names and key words yourself. 3. Paste your transcript and ask AI for 3 stronger opening lines. Pick the best one for your first 2 seconds. 4. Have AI find 3 short clips worth posting inside one long video. 5. Get 5 title ideas and a short description, then edit them so they sound like you. **Where this fits:** The owner still teaches filming, story and style. This drop just shows a few ways to get the editing done faster. **Ways to use it for engagement:** - **Poll:** "Which of these 5 have you tried? Pick all that apply." - **Before-and-after challenge:** "Edit one Short using just one of the 5 ideas. Post the old and new version." - **Day-3 follow-up:** "Which one saved you the most time? Which one was a waste? Be honest." **Supplementary content:** a checklist ("Edit a Short in 15 minutes") and a copy-paste prompt for idea #3. ### EXAMPLE DROP 3 (quick): Local-business coaching group > **Example only.** **The Concept: "The 5-second neighbour test for your Google Business Profile"** Could a stranger tell in 5 seconds what you do, where you are, and when you're open? If not, fix the top of the profile first: business description, main category, hours, and a real photo of your place or your work. - **Engagement posts:** "Post your profile's first line. The group gives it the 5-second test." · Poll: "When did you last update your profile? A) This month B) This year C) Um..." · Day-3 follow-up: "Did you change one thing? Post it." - **Supplementary content:** a 10-point profile checklist and a prompt that rewrites a business description in plain language. ## Why "jack of all trades" is the niche Jack has 25 years of local-business marketing, an MBA in digital marketing, a banker's eye for what makes money, and years of farming, where you fix whatever breaks. Most suppliers pick one topic. Jack's range lets one format serve many groups. It just needs the right packaging. ### One format, many niche editions The three parts (concept, engagement posts, supplementary content) stay the same every week. What changes is the niche edition. Each edition is the same for every buyer in that niche, so it stays a product, not custom work. ### Same concept, angled for different niches Example: this week's core idea is **"Get 5 uses out of one piece of work."**
Niche edition How the concept is angled
AI / OpenClaw owners Turn one agent output (a report or summary) into 5 useful pieces for your business
Video / YouTube Turn one long video into 5 Shorts, with a hook for each
Local-business coaching Turn one happy customer review into a post, a sign, an email line, a web quote and a thank-you card
General community owners Turn one member win into a welcome example, a post, a lesson example, a testimonial and a Friday shout-out
### How to pick which niches to supply first - **Beachhead: small-to-mid paid Skool owners (50–1,000 members).** They have the pain (a feed to keep alive) and the money (paying members). They sit below the top earners. For context, it takes about \$49K MRR to crack the Skool leaderboard's top 100. The owners below that line are the big, under-served middle. They're openly asking for post templates and a 30-day calendar (Skool research, Sep 28, 2026). - **Start with 1 edition, then add 1 at a time.** Only add an edition when the one before it ships on time and at good quality. - **Candidate editions, in suggested order:** 1. **Local-business coaching.** Jack's home turf. Instant credibility. 2. **AI / OpenClaw.** Fast-moving, so owners need a fresh "what matters this week" angle. Risk: many new groups are free (the largest OpenClaw group is \~875 members and free), so look for the paid ones. On Facebook, the biggest OpenClaw/AI groups are much larger (100K to 450K members) and also free. Their owners are a second buyer type to test (see the Sep 28 section below). 3. **Video / content creators.** Lots of practical, tool-driven tips that change often. ### Buyer segments (ranked) Ranked from best to weakest fit. The ratings are judgment calls, not data.
Rank Buyer segment Why they'd buy Ability to pay Ease of reach Fit with Jack
1 **Small-to-mid paid Skool owners (50–1,000 members)** They have paying members to keep, but no team. Finding one fresh, useful thing a week is a big job, and they're already asking for templates and calendars. Good. They already earn monthly revenue, so a small tool is easy to justify. High. They gather in the Skoolers community and around Skool Games. Strong. Business-minded owners respect a marketer with 25 years in the trenches.

Mid-size paid groups exist too (e.g., AI Money Group, \~455 members at \$49/mo). High at the top, mixed below. High. Very active online. Medium to strong. Secondary (to test) **Large free Facebook AI/OpenClaw group owners (100K to 450K members)** Huge groups with no priced owner offer and nothing to hand members each week.
