## What the Facebook research changes (Sep 28) *Source: Social Shit's read-only Facebook research, Sep 28, 2026. These are partial feed samples (about 10 to 20 posts per group), not full reads.* Details and links: ### 1. A second buyer type: owners of the big free Facebook AI groups The biggest OpenClaw and AI groups on Facebook have 100K to 450K members (for example, groups with 451K, 428K, 154K, 123K and 103K members). None of them showed a priced owner offer, and none had anything to hand members each week. The owners have the attention but no product. - A weekly concept drop gives them something to post every week. - It could also become their first product. For example, the owner gates the drop behind an opt-in, so members sign up to get it. - In one big group only the owner may sell, and another blocks links in posts. Going through the owner is the clean way in. - **Status: secondary, to test.** These are free groups, so nobody has shown they will pay for this. See the buyer table above and Risks below. ### 2. Format proof: "Comment WORD, get the asset" Posts that say "comment a word and I'll send you the thing" got far more comments than normal posts: - An n8n template bundle post in AI Hub (154K members): 211 comments - A CRM giveaway: 131 comments - A Hermes "PACK" post: 73 comments Almost all of these were posted by members, not owners. The owners are not using the format themselves yet. So every weekly drop now includes **one comment-to-get post**. The owner posts it, members comment the keyword, and the supplementary content is what they get. This ties the three parts together: the concept is the reason to care, the post gets the comments, and the extras are the prize. See the updated "What's in each weekly drop" section and Example Drop 1. ### 3. The OpenClaw edition fits Jack's own experience What members struggle with most: - Updates breaking their setup - The agent losing memory or context - Hand-offs between agents - Capping how many tool calls an agent gets - Installs crashing on small servers - Local hardware questions - Beginners asking for a roadmap Searches found zero shares of `SOUL.md` files, skill files or agent configs. Nobody is supplying ready configs, hand-off checklists, memory-cleanup routines or health checks. Jack runs about 15 AI agents on OpenClaw across 4 servers and has fought crashes and updates for about 8 months. He has lived these problems. So he isn't pitching as an AI guru. He's the "finish the edges so it doesn't crack" guy from the driveway story. The owner still teaches AI. Jack hands over the tip that keeps the setup from cracking. **Example weekly concept titles for the OpenClaw edition (example ideas only):** 1. Before you hit update: a 5-minute backup routine 2. Why your agent forgot everything, and the weekly cleanup that fixes it 3. A simple hand-off checklist between two agents 4. Set a tool-call cap so one task can't run away 5. A 10-minute weekly health check for your agents ## Why owners need this (background research) ### The problem owners face - **Feeds go quiet.** After launch week, posts get fewer replies. A quiet feed tells new members the group is dead. - **Churn.** Members leave once they finish a course, unless something new and useful keeps coming. - **Pressure to produce every week.** Grok Research found that the top AI Skool groups make \$200K+ MRR on about 2.5k–3.5k members by selling a result. That means owners must keep producing fresh, usable material every week. That's the supplier gap. - **Platform limits.** Skool owners can't schedule posts, and "email all members" is capped at once every 72 hours. So every post has to be ready, simple, and worth it. - **Burnout.** Most owners are also running a business, coaching, or working a job. Ideas run dry fast. ### What Skool research shows (Skool research, Sep 28, 2026) - **Engagement beats more content.** In the Skoolers community, a retention thread by Tommy Driscoll (89 comments) landed on this point. That's why each drop is one concept plus posts that get replies, not a pile of content. - **Owners are asking for ready-made material:** post templates, a ready-made 30-day content calendar, and design templates. Course templates reportedly stopped churn among affiliates. - **Themed weeks work.** AI Money Group (Jeff Hunter, \~455 members, \$49/mo) runs a themed week: Money Monday, tool days, Proof Friday, Set-and-Forget Saturday, Sunday Reset, plus a Tuesday mission call. This supports the Engagement Kit add-on below. - **Homework / mission threads and the "Start Here" post beat news posts.** - **Top groups keep members with time-based unlocks and weekly calls.** Example: AIS+ unlocks a client module at 30 days and a scale module at 90 days. ### Why supply beats being another guru - The guru market is crowded and loud. Everyone is selling "how to grow your Skool." - Owners don't need another course. They need something they can **use today**. - A supplier doesn't compete with the gurus. The gurus' students are our buyers. - Jack doesn't need to be famous or a great writer. AI does the drafting. Jack needs a good eye for what's useful, which he has. - Supply is repeatable: the same product every week for many buyers, with no client calls. ## How it's made each week AI agents do the research and the writing. Jack doesn't write the drops. He picks, checks, and adds a line of real-world experience where it helps. ### Weekly pipeline (core drop)
Step Who What happens
1. Watch Research agent Scans each niche for what's new and useful: tool updates, release notes, common questions in public owner forums and group feeds, seasonal hooks. Suggests 3 concept ideas per edition.
2. Pick **Jack** Picks the week's concept. Checks it won't step on what the target groups already teach.
3. Draft Writing agent Drafts the concept, the "where this fits" note, 2–4 engagement posts, and the supplementary pieces.
4. Angle Writing agent Adapts the concept for each niche edition.
5. Design Design agent Makes the graphic or fills a Canva template.
6. Review **Jack** Reads the concept, fixes anything off, and adds his own experience. Spot-checks the posts and extras.
7. QC QC agent Checks facts against sources, flags "AI slop" phrases, grade-8 reading level, repeats of past weeks, broken links.
8. Ship Delivery agent Uploads to the vault and sends the delivery note on drop day.
### Jack's weekly time (estimates, to test)
Task Estimated time
Pick the concept 10–15 min
Review the concept and add his experience 30–45 min
Spot-check each extra niche edition about 15 min per edition
Approve and ship 5 min
Read buyer ratings and notes 15 min
**Total** **About 1–1.5 hours for the first edition, plus about 15 min for each added edition (estimate)**
### Quality control - Facts in "what's new" concepts must link to a real source. If it can't be checked, it doesn't ship. - A banned-phrase list (e.g., "unlock your potential," "in today's fast-paced world"). - A "would a good owner post this in their own group?" test on every concept. - A tracker so no concept repeats within 6 months. - Buyer feedback: a 1-click "did this get replies?" rating on each drop. ### Delivery - **Email:** A short weekly delivery note with a link and a "start here" line. This is a delivery note, **not** a newsletter. No essays from Jack. - **Vault (Skool classroom or Notion):** Every past drop is stored and searchable by niche and type (concepts, posts, prompts, checklists). - **Maybe a Skool group of its own, with the feed mostly off:** Used as a delivery shelf, not a community. Jack doesn't host or moderate it. ### Licensing
License What the buyer can do
**Personal use** Use in your own group(s). Edit freely. Post as your own.
**Done-for-you rights** Use in groups you run for clients (for community managers and agencies).
**White-label / resell rights** Put your own brand on it and hand it to your members or clients. Resell rights also spread our distribution (see Distribution). No resale as a competing weekly drop.
## Offer and pricing ladder options > **All prices are hypotheses to test**, not decisions. ### What the market charges now (sellers' own numbers, via Grok Research)
Comparable Cadence Price
Secret Weapon PLR Weekly \~\$27/mo
Quick Content Club Monthly pack \$27/mo
Content Strategy Studio Monthly pack \$47/mo
PLR Pass 2 packages a month \$67
Template Skool (Skool supplier group, \~3.6k members) Library \$69/yr
Evelyn Weiss's coach hub (resell rights) Monthly \$7/mo
**What this tells us:** Owners pay for ready-to-use material but spend little, so these sellers rely on volume. Monthly packs are common. Weekly drops are rarer, so **weekly is a differentiator**. The sweet spot for an entry tier looks like about \$27/mo. ### Proposed ladder
Tier What's included Test price (hypothesis)
**Weekly Drop (entry, the core)** One concept a week in one niche edition, 2–4 engagement posts, the supplementary content, the vault, the 30-day calendar welcome bonus, personal-use license \$19–\$29 / month (anchor test at \$27)
**Drop + Engagement Kit (Pro, the upsell)** Everything in Weekly Drop + the Weekly Engagement Kit add-on (themed-day plan, see below) + access to all niche editions + editable Canva files + done-for-you rights \$47–\$79 / month
**White-label / Agency** Everything in Pro + white-label / resell rights + multi-group use \$149–\$299 / month
Optional tests (all hypotheses): a **one-time "starter crate"** (the first 4 drops bundled) at \$27–\$47, an **annual plan** (the \$69/yr Template Skool price shows some owners prefer a yearly buy), and the **Engagement Kit as a stand-alone add-on** priced in the gap between Entry and Pro. **Consistency with the Aug 31 rules:** - One product, the same for everyone. Niche editions are also the same for everyone in that niche. - **No custom client work.** No "we'll write it for your group" option. - **Nothing puts Jack in a client's weekly inbox as a service provider.** The weekly email is a product delivery note, not a service or a newsletter. - No calls, no coaching, no retainer. (The call run sheet in the add-on is for the owner's own call. Jack never runs it.) ## Add-on: Weekly Engagement Kit (cross-sell) This was the core product in the first version of this page. It's now an add-on for owners who want a full week of posts, not just the concept. It sells in the Pro tier (or as a stand-alone add-on, to test). The kit is built around the week's concept where it fits, so the two work together. ### The weekly cadence: a themed-day plan Modeled on what works in top groups (themed days, mission threads, a weekly call, Friday proof). The owner copies and posts each day's piece, since Skool can't schedule posts.
Day Theme What the owner posts
**Sunday (drop day)** Reset The kit lands (email + vault) with the week's concept. Optional "Sunday Reset" post: "What's your focus this week?"
**Monday** Monday prompt The week's standout discussion prompt + poll. Kicks off the mission.
**Tuesday** Mission call Live-call topic + 30-minute run sheet.
**Wednesday (day 3)** Midweek mission check-in The **second use**: a check-in on the mission. Pulls in members who missed Monday.
**Thursday** Tool / tip day A quick resource or tip post from the bonus content.
**Friday** Proof / wins A proof-or-wins thread: members post what they finished.
**Next Sunday** Fresh kit.
Each kit also includes **one "email all" message** for the week, because Skool caps email-all at once every 72 hours. ### What's in the kit **1. MAIN: "Here's what you need this week that you can just use in your group"** Each week has **one standout piece** (marked "Start here"), with supporting pieces around it: - **Monday discussion prompt** + 3 follow-up replies the owner can use to keep the thread going - **A poll** tied to the week's theme - **A mission / homework thread** with a **day-3 check-in** post (mission threads beat news posts) - **A Friday proof / wins thread starter** - **A live-call topic + run sheet** (30 minutes, timed) - **A welcome / "Start Here" post refresh** and onboarding script for new members - **A re-engagement DM** for quiet members - **A time-based unlock idea** (e.g., what to unlock at 30 days) to give members a reason to stay after the course - **The week's "email all" message** (one per week, to fit Skool's 72-hour cap) - **Graphics or a Canva template** for the prompt, mission and wins posts **2. LIGHT: A little "how to grow your group"** Kept small and at the back, so we don't fight the gurus: - **One small tactic a week**, in 5 lines or less. Example: "Add one question to your join form that tells you what to post about." **3. BONUS: Content that helps in their group** - **A short lesson** (a 5-minute read or talking points) - **A swipe file** (e.g., 10 post hooks) - **A checklist** - **A mini-module** they can drop into their Skool classroom (useful as a locked or time-based unlock) ### EXAMPLE: A fully worked sample kit week > **This is an example only**, to show the format. Theme: **"The One-Thing Week"** **Start here (the standout piece): The "One Thing" Mission** - **Monday post:** "Quick one: What's ONE thing you'll finish by Friday? Not five. One. Drop it below and I'll check back Wednesday. 👇" - **3 follow-ups for the owner:** 1. "Love it. What's the first 15-minute step?" 2. "What usually gets in the way of this one?" 3. "Who else here is working on something similar? Tag them." - **Tuesday mission call (30 min):** 0–5 welcome and early wins · 5–15 hot seat: two members share their one thing and what's blocking it · 15–25 group fixes · 25–30 everyone commits to a Wednesday update. - **Day-3 check-in (Wednesday):** "Halfway check. How's your ONE thing going? Reply with 🟢 on track, 🟡 slipping, or 🔴 stuck. If you're 🔴, tell us why and we'll help." - **Thursday tip:** "The 15-minute rule: if it takes under 15 minutes, do it now. Post one thing you knocked out today." - **Friday proof thread:** "Proof Friday. Did you finish your ONE thing? Post it, even if it's small. Finished beats perfect." **Poll (Monday):** "What steals most of your focus? A) Email B) Social media C) Meetings D) My own ideas" **Email-all message (send Monday):** "This week we're doing the One Thing Mission. Pick one goal, post it in the group, and we'll check in Wednesday. Takes 30 seconds: \[link\]" **Welcome script (new members this week):** "Welcome, \[Name\]! Good timing. We're doing the One Thing Mission this week. Start with the pinned Start Here post, then tell us your one thing." **Re-engagement DM:** "Hey \[Name\], haven't seen you in a bit. We're doing a quick mission this week. No pressure, just one goal. Want in? Here's the post: \[link\]" **Unlock idea:** Members who post Monday **and** check in Wednesday unlock a bonus resource, and a "Focus Toolkit" module unlocks at 30 days. **Graphic:** Canva template: "My ONE Thing This Week: \[blank\]" (square, for posts). **Growth tip (light):** "Pin the mission post and mention it in your Start Here post. New members join a live activity, not an empty feed." **Bonus content:** - Short lesson: "Why one goal beats five" (talking points) - Checklist: "Plan your week in 10 minutes" - Mini-module: "The Weekly Focus Routine" (3 short lessons, ready to drop into the classroom) ### Kit production pipeline
Step Who What happens
1. Watch Research agent Scans trends, top Skool groups' public feeds and leaderboards, owner forums (like Skoolers), and seasonal hooks. Suggests 3 theme ideas that pair with the week's concept.
2. Pick **Jack** Chooses the week's theme.
3. Draft Writing agent Drafts the full kit: Monday prompt + follow-ups, poll, mission + day-3 check-in, call run sheet, Friday wins thread, scripts, email-all message, growth tip, bonus content.
4. Design Design agent Makes graphics and fills Canva templates.
5. Format Formatting agent Formats for Skool (copy-paste-ready posts, day by day), the vault, and the delivery email. Builds niche editions by swapping examples.
6. Review **Jack** Reviews and polishes **the one standout piece**. Spot-checks the rest.
7. QC QC agent Checks for generic "AI slop" phrases, reading level (grade 8), repeats of past weeks, broken links, and license notes.
8. Ship Delivery agent Uploads to the vault and sends with the core drop on drop day.
### Tools (candidates, to confirm) - An LLM for drafting (Jack's agent fleet) - Canva (templates and graphics) - Notion (production board and/or vault) - Skool classroom (vault / delivery shelf) - An email tool for the weekly delivery note - A simple checkout / payments tool ### Human-in-the-loop points 1. **Theme pick** (Jack) 2. **Standout piece review** (Jack). This is where quality lives. 3. **Final approve-to-ship** (Jack, one click) ### Quality control (kit) - A banned-phrase list (e.g., "unlock your potential," "in today's fast-paced world"). - A "would I post this in my own group?" test on the standout piece. - A tracker so no prompt or mission repeats within 6 months. - Buyer feedback: a 1-click "did this get replies?" rating on each kit. ### Extra weekly time for Jack if the kit is offered (estimate)
Task Estimated time
Pick the theme 10 min
Review and polish the standout piece 45–60 min
Spot-check the rest of the kit 20 min
Approve and ship 5 min
**Total** **About 1.5 hours a week on top of the core drop (estimate)**
## Distribution ideas How community owners could find it, without Jack hosting a group or writing a newsletter: - **Free sample drop:** One full weekly drop (concept + posts + extras) as a lead magnet. Let owners feel the "crack a beer" moment. - **Free 30-day calendar:** Owners are explicitly asking for one. Give a sample away as the top-of-funnel hook, and use it to show the Engagement Kit add-on. - **Skool's owner hangouts:** Be useful in places like the Skoolers community (e.g., retention threads) and around Skool Games (value posts, sample concepts, no hard pitching). - **Affiliate deals with group owners and gurus:** Pay a recurring commission to people who teach community building. Their students are our buyers, so we're a partner, not a rival. - **Resell rights as a distribution engine:** A paid resell tier lets other sellers carry the product to their buyers. Evelyn Weiss's \$7/mo hub claims 5,359+ coaches, and Template Tribe runs a resell-rights paid tier. - **Bundle partners:** Get included in community-launch bundles or tool deals (e.g., alongside scheduling or community-management tools). - **Owner forums and subreddits:** Answer "what do I post?" questions with a real sample concept and a link. - **Marketplace listings:** List the free sample and starter crate on digital-product marketplaces and PLR stores. - **Niche edition outreach:** Short, direct outreach to owners in each niche (starting with local-business coaching) with a free sample drop from their edition. ## What already exists From a quick web search (Sep 28, 2026), , and Skool research (Sep 28, 2026). All numbers are the sellers' own claims. ### PLR and content subscriptions
Product What it is Source
**Secret Weapon PLR** Weekly PLR drops, \~\$27/mo. One of the few weekly sellers. Grok Research
**Quick Content Club** Monthly content pack, \$27/mo. Grok Research
**Content Strategy Studio** Monthly content pack, \$47/mo. Grok Research
**PLR Pass** 2 packages a month for \$67. Grok Research
[**PLR.me**](http://PLR.me) Has run 18+ years; claims 600K+ creators. Grok Research
**Boundless PLR: 50+ Membership Site Content AI Prompts** One-time PLR/MRR pack of Canva-editable prompts for membership owners. [shop.boundlessplr.com](https://shop.boundlessplr.com/products/50-membership-content-ai-prompts)
**Marketing Sharks: "Build Your Paid Community at Skool" AI PLR** A PLR ebook about building paid Skool communities. [marketingsharks.com](https://www.marketingsharks.com/build-your-paid-community-at-skool/)
### Supplier groups on Skool that sell to owners
Product What it is Source
**Template Skool** \~3.6k members, \$69/yr. Grok Research
**Template Tribe** \~3.3k members, with a paid tier that includes resell rights. Grok Research
**Skool Copy Hub** Copy and templates for Skool owners. Grok Research
**School For Skool** Sells \$97 "Ready Kits" (course structure, engagement prompts, launch copy), plus custom course work (\$297) and custom builds (\$997+). [skool.com/school-for-skool-6921](https://www.skool.com/school-for-skool-6921)
### Engagement templates and tools
Product What it is Source
**StickyHive** Free engagement-template library for Skool, Circle and Mighty Networks (says 1,000+), a free Skool prompt generator, and paid scheduling/automation. [Templates](https://stickyhive.ai/community-engagement-templates/) · [Prompt generator](https://stickyhive.ai/skool/free-tools/engagement-prompts/) · [GitHub](https://github.com/stickyhive/skool-community-management-templates)
**Lilach Bullock: Community Engagement Prompt Pack / Content Calendar** Copy-paste prompt pack and a 30-day community content calendar. [Prompt pack](https://www.lilachbullock.com/resources/community-engagement-prompt-pack/) · [Calendar](https://www.lilachbullock.com/resources/community-content-calendar-template/)
**BuddyActivity content templates** Niche content packs (15–60 days of posts) for BuddyBoss communities. [buddyactivity.com/templates](https://buddyactivity.com/templates)
**Evelyn Weiss's coach hub** \$7/mo hub with resell rights; claims 5,359+ coaches. Grok Research
### Models to learn from (not competitors) - **AI Money Group** (Jeff Hunter, \~455 members, \$49/mo): themed week (Money Monday, tool days, Proof Friday, Set-and-Forget Saturday, Sunday Reset) plus a Tuesday mission call. Skool research, Sep 28, 2026. - **AIS+**: time-based unlocks (client module at 30 days, scale module at 90). Skool research, Sep 28, 2026. **What this tells us:** The market is real and proven ([PLR.me](http://PLR.me)'s long run, supplier groups with thousands of members). But most offers are generic templates, monthly packs, or big libraries, and some are free. Almost none hand an owner **one fresh, niche-specific concept each week** with ready posts to run it. That's the gap. Themed-day engagement kits exist in pieces, which is why the kit works better as an add-on than as the main product. ## Risks and open questions - **Stepping on the owner's expertise.** If a concept overlaps what the owner already teaches, or contradicts it, it makes them look bad. Every drop needs a "where this fits" note, and Jack's pick step must check for overlap. - **Niche breadth can make quality uneven.** Jack knows local business deeply, but not every niche equally. Launch one edition at a time, source-check every "what's new" concept, and only add an edition when the last one is solid. - **Fast-moving topics go stale.** An AI "what's new" concept can be out of date in a week. Ship close to drop day and link sources. - **PLR is crowded and cheap.** Buyers may see this as "just more PLR." We need to show it's different: one concept, niche-specific, weekly, with ready posts. - **Free alternatives exist.** StickyHive's free templates and free AI tools set a low bar. Why pay? (Answer to test: curation, freshness, and a niche angle the owner didn't have time to find.) - **Quality vs. generic AI slop.** If a drop reads like a chatbot wrote it, we lose trust fast. Jack's review is the moat, and it has to be real. - **Proving the engagement lift.** We need before/after proof (replies, active members) from early users. How do we collect it without doing client work? - **Willingness to pay.** Will owners pay monthly, yearly, or only buy once? Does the kit upsell sell? - **Big free Facebook groups may not pay.** The large OpenClaw/AI group owners (100K to 450K members) are a second buyer type to test, but their groups are free and none showed a priced offer. They may like the drop and still not pay for it. Test with one or two owners before building for them. The Facebook research was also a partial sample (about 10 to 20 posts per group). - **Owner's voice.** Can shared material feel like the owner's own voice? How much editing will they need? - **Platform limits and risk.** No post scheduling and a 72-hour email-all cap mean owners post by hand. Skool may change features. Drops should work on any platform. - **The working name.** "Shovel Your Biz-Shit" is memorable but may put off some buyers or marketplaces. Test it, and keep "Shovels for Community Builders" as a clean fallback. ## Next steps 1. **Validate demand with research.** Finish the page (in progress): owner pain, current tools, price points, where owners gather. 2. **Build 2 sample drops** with the AI pipeline: one local-business-coaching edition and one AI / OpenClaw edition (using a real, checked update). Time Jack's review. 3. **Build 1 sample Engagement Kit week** to test as the add-on. 4. **Test the free sample drop** with 10–20 small-to-mid paid Skool owners. Ask: "Did you post it? Did it fit your group? Did it get replies? Would you pay?" 5. **Run a price test** on the entry tier (e.g., \$19 vs. \$27 on a simple landing page), and see how many take the kit upsell. 6. **Line up 2–3 affiliate or resell-rights conversations** with community-building teachers and supplier groups. 7. **Decide go / no-go** based on sample usage and pre-orders.

Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/e58507cea4684c25a65f37a03e67bdb4 as of 2026-09-29T04:56:23.468Z: {"title":"NotionAI-Thoughts"} null ## Overview The work under Perfect Product is converging on a quiet, productized supplier business rather than another community, newsletter, coaching offer, or software-specific product. The strongest direction is to supply repeatable, ready-to-use campaigns and assets to people who already own an audience. They bring the customers, trust, and delivery channel. ZedBiz brings the practical idea, finished materials, production system, and quality control. This uses Jack's real strength: cross-domain practical judgment. He does not have to become the public expert on one tool, perform online every day, or educate thousands of end buyers. AI and automation remain production tools behind the scenes rather than the headline. The immediate goal should not be to build a large subscription library. It should be to prove that one standardized campaign creates a measurable result for several similar buyers. If that works, the campaign can become recurring inventory and eventually a transferable business system. ## Three key thoughts ### 1. Build a wholesale product factory The better question is not, “What should Jack sell to thousands of people?” It is, “Who already has customers and repeatedly needs something useful to deliver or sell to them?” Potential buyers include: - Paid community and membership owners - Local publishers and directory operators - Associations - Coaches with established audiences - Agencies that need client-facing assets The channel owner should be treated as the customer, not merely an affiliate. ZedBiz supplies finished inventory that the owner can deliver under their own name. Their members may never need to know ZedBiz exists. This removes the hardest unsolved problem: Jack personally manufacturing attention from zero. ### 2. Sell a measurable campaign, not “weekly content” A weekly drop is a delivery method, not a strong product promise. “Fresh content every week” is too easy to compare with cheap PLR and free AI output. The initial product should be a fixed four-week campaign built around a measurable operating result, such as: - Reactivate quiet members - Give new members a useful first win - Produce credible member success stories - Keep members active after they finish a course - Turn existing members into leads for the owner's next offer The weekly concept, posts, checklist, comment-to-get asset, and supporting material become components of that campaign. The first commercial test should be the same four-week campaign sold to three established owners. If it creates a measurable result, the recurring subscription becomes the replenishment plan. This proves value before creating another endless production commitment. ### 3. Build performance intelligence as the moat AI can generate posts, prompts, templates, and checklists. A content vault by itself will become increasingly commoditized. The valuable asset is the evidence showing what causes each type of audience to act. Every campaign should capture: - Whether the owner actually posted each item - Replies and participation generated - Member actions or completed challenges - Leads or sales produced - The owner's rating and comments - What failed and under what conditions Over time, this creates a private performance dataset and operating playbook. The agents can generate candidates, the system can select ideas using accumulated evidence, and Jack can review exceptions rather than write everything. That is what makes the business defensible and sellable. A future buyer could acquire the production process, customer licenses, performance data, and operating rules without depending on Jack's personality or daily presence. ## Recommended next move - Select one class of established audience owner. - Define one measurable four-week result they already care about. - Sell the identical pilot to three owners before building a subscription library. - Track usage and outcomes from every component. - Turn the winning campaign into recurring inventory. - Codify Jack's review decisions so another trained operator can eventually run the system. The emerging business is a quiet, white-label supplier for people who already own attention. The long-term asset is not a pile of content. It is a measured system for repeatedly creating material that gets a specific audience to act. ## Trial phase The cleanest first test is a four-week Member Wake-Up Campaign for paid community owners. Do not build a subscription yet. Prove that owners will use the material and that members respond. ### Pick one beachhead Start with owners of paid communities serving local-business owners, marketers, or practical operators. Reasons to start here: - Jack understands their members. - The owner already earns recurring revenue. - An inactive member has a visible financial cost. - Owners need fresh reasons for members to return. - They can test the campaign without technical setup. ### Float the problem before pitching the product Post about the pain and result, not the product name. Test three angles over seven days. **Post A: Problem test** > Paid community owners, quick question. What is harder right now: getting new members or getting existing members to come back and participate? I’m looking at a simple four-week system for waking up quiet members without adding more live calls or another course. Curious which problem is actually costing owners more. **Post B: Behaviour test** > If I handed you a complete member-engagement campaign every Monday, what would make you actually use it? A) Ready-to-post discussion
B) Member challenge
C) Comment-to-get resource
D) Re-engagement message
E) A full weekly campaign built around one result **Post C: Offer test** > I’m looking for three paid-community owners to test a four-week Member Wake-Up Campaign. You get one complete campaign each week: the main post, follow-ups, a member action, a downloadable resource, and a simple results tracker. No consulting, no new software, and no extra calls. You post it inside your existing community and report what happened. Comment WAKE-UP or message me if you have a paid group with at least 50 members. Use LinkedIn, relevant Facebook groups where promotion is allowed, and direct messages to community owners Jack already knows. ### Measure buying signals, not ordinary engagement Likes from marketers and AI enthusiasts are weak evidence. Measure: - Qualified community owners responding - Owners volunteering information about their problem - Requests to see the sample - Owners willing to install the campaign - Owners willing to pay The first gate should be: - 20 targeted owner conversations - At least five requests for a sample - Three pilot customers - At least two willing to pay Charge US\$99 to US\$149 for the complete four-week founding pilot. Free testers frequently praise products they never use. A paid pilot proves the problem matters. ### Trial success criteria Continue only if: - At least two of three owners complete the four weeks. - Owners post at least 75% of the supplied material. - At least half the campaign posts beat the community’s normal participation. - Owners report meaningful preparation time saved. - At least two owners want another month. - Jack’s review and support stay below two hours per week. If owners buy but do not post, the product is too difficult or does not match their workflow. If they post but members do not act, the campaign is weak. If members act but owners will not renew, the financial outcome is unclear. ## Building the MVP ### MVP offer **Working name:** Member Wake-Up Campaign **Promise:** > Wake up quiet members and create four visible wins in four weeks, without adding another course or live call. This is stronger than selling “weekly content” because it names a result. ### Build only Week One before selling Create one complete sample containing: - One practical weekly concept - One primary discussion or mission post - Three short owner replies to keep the discussion moving - One day-three follow-up - One comment-to-get resource - One Friday proof or wins post - One re-engagement message for inactive members - One small graphic - One results form For Weeks Two through Four, prepare titles and short outlines only. Finish them after the first pilots pay and provide baseline information. ### Suggested four-week campaign **Week One: Return** Give inactive members a tiny, low-pressure reason to show up again. **Week Two: Complete** Run one small challenge members can finish within the week. **Week Three: Prove** Turn completed work into screenshots, examples, testimonials, or member wins. **Week Four: Continue** Move participants toward the owner’s next module, offer, event, or renewal reason. This creates a clear progression rather than four disconnected content packs. ### Simple delivery system Use existing tools: - Notion for the customer portal and campaign vault - GHL or email for weekly delivery notifications - Canva for one reusable graphic template - Notion Forms or Google Forms for weekly owner feedback - A Notion database for results and performance tracking Each pilot receives the same core campaign. Only allow light substitutions such as terminology, niche examples, and the owner’s call to action. Do not create a different campaign for every customer. ### Track the moat from day one For every campaign component, record: - Delivered - Posted or not posted - Date posted - Normal engagement baseline - Comments or replies - Members completing the action - Leads or sales produced - Owner rating - Time saved - Would use again - Owner’s exact objection or requested change This is how the MVP becomes a real system rather than another content service. ### Do not build yet Avoid: - A full website - A new Skool community - A large content vault - Multiple niche editions - Automated personalization - White-label software - An affiliate program - Annual subscriptions - Fifty templates - Custom client campaigns Sell and complete three identical pilots first. ## Immediate move Create one polished Week One sample, publish the three social posts, and directly approach 20 qualified community owners. The key question is not whether people like the concept. It is: > Will an established owner pay, post the material, get a visible response, and ask for the next campaign? If the answer is yes three times, build the subscription.

## Overview
The Perfect Product work is converging on something broader than finding one clever offer. The strongest opportunity may be to combine three layers: a repeatable product-manufacturing capability, a recurring product that removes a real weekly obligation for the buyer, and distribution through people who already own the audience.
The key shift is to stop treating AI, OpenClaw, GoHighLevel, agents, research, templates, and content as things Jack must sell directly. They can become the manufacturing infrastructure behind the product. The customer buys the finished result, not the machinery.
This direction also fits the four Perfect Product bars: repeat/revenue potential, build-once leverage, creation of a sellable asset, and reduced dependence on Jack's daily presence. It also addresses the recurring problems found throughout the research: Jack does not want to be a community host or influencer, local businesses often require too much education and onboarding, and building a new audience from scratch makes otherwise-good products economically weak.
## The three strategic thoughts
### The product may actually be a Weekly Operating System, not content
The Shovel Your Biz-Shit concept is closer to the opportunity than it first appears, but the product should not be framed as content for community owners.
The real promise is:
> **You never have to figure out what useful thing you're giving your customers or members this week.**
That is an operational dependency rather than a content subscription.
Instead of selling a concept, several posts, a checklist, prompt, or graphic as separate pieces, the product can become a completed weekly campaign-in-a-box. The buyer opens it and thinks: **Good. This week is handled.**
A weekly kit could contain the teaching piece, engagement piece, downloadable asset, follow-up, email, graphic, and short video script. The exact components matter less than eliminating the recurring job.
This also suggests the market should not be restricted to Skool or community owners. The same underlying product could potentially serve:
- Membership owners
- Coaches
- Associations
- Franchises
- SaaS companies educating customers
- Agencies serving a vertical
- Newsletters and publishers
- Chambers
- Vendors with dealer networks
A useful category description may be **Recurring Customer-Value Kits**.
The strategic distinction is important: we are not helping customers create more content. We are taking ownership of one recurring obligation in their business. That should improve retention because cancelling means the weekly job lands back on their desk.
### Stop looking only for Jack's perfect niche and find the perfect distributor
Much of the research asks: **Who should Jack sell to?**
A potentially more valuable question is:
> **Who already owns 1,000–100,000 of the people who should use this product?**
The Carex Hip Kit is an important clue. Its strength is not merely the bundle. It enters an existing medical distribution system at the moment the buyer needs it.
Distribution therefore may deserve to become a fifth bar of the Perfect Product definition rather than merely one desirable trait.
A strong inexpensive product with no distribution can remain a hobby. A fairly ordinary inexpensive product embedded in somebody else's established distribution can become a substantial business.
Instead of designing only for:
**Jack → thousands of individual customers**
we should deliberately investigate:
**Jack → a small number of distributors → hundreds or thousands of end customers**
Potential distributors could include Skool consultants, associations, software companies, niche publishers, agencies, industry suppliers, directories, franchise systems, and creators with large audiences but weak recurring offers.
White-label or licensed versions deserve serious consideration. The distributor keeps the audience, relationship, and brand. ZedBiz becomes the supplier behind the scenes.
That model fits Jack particularly well because he does not need to become the influencer, niche celebrity, or community personality. **Jack/ZedBiz can be the factory.**
### We may be building a Product Factory rather than searching for one Perfect Product
The research continues to ask what specific thing should be produced each week. A different approach is to build the machine capable of repeatedly discovering and producing narrowly targeted products.
ZedBiz already has much of the raw infrastructure:
- Multiple AI models and agents
- Research capability
- Content and marketing capability
- Automation
- GoHighLevel and WordPress
- Canva and creative production
- Templates, prompts, checklists, workflows, and graphics
- Decades of practical business and marketing experience
The more valuable long-term asset may therefore be a **ZedBiz Product Engine**.
Its basic pipeline could be:
**Market → current problem → research → useful concept → practical asset → campaign → QA → packaged product → market test**
That engine could manufacture many kinds of products:
- Weekly community/customer kits
- Association member kits
- Seasonal local-business kits
- OpenClaw operator packs
- Marketing kits
- WordPress packs
- Rural-business packs
- Promotion kits
- Decision kits
Most experiments do not need to become permanent businesses. The advantage of the engine is that product hypotheses can be produced and tested inexpensively.
This changes the strategic objective from:
> **Discover the Perfect Product before committing.**
to:
> **Build a system that can repeatedly discover Perfect Products through real market evidence.**
When one product starts selling disproportionately well, that is when we narrow the focus, automate production, add recurring revenue, recruit distribution partners, deepen the moat, and turn it into a sellable standalone asset.
## Combined direction
The strongest combined thesis coming out of this review is:
> **Product Factory → Recurring Operating Kit → Distributed through people who already own the audience.**
This structure addresses several problems that have repeatedly killed earlier ideas:
- Jack does not need to become a guru.
- Jack does not need to host another community.
- ZedBiz does not need to build a huge audience before making sales.
- AI infrastructure gains a direct economic purpose without AI itself needing to be the offer.
- New product ideas can be tested rather than debated indefinitely.
- Successful products can eventually become independent sellable assets.
The most important conceptual shift is that the agents, AI models, automation, GHL, research systems, and creative tools are potentially **the manufacturing floor — not the product being sold.**
That may be the clearest role yet for the infrastructure ZedBiz has been building.
## Trial Phase and MVP
The next move should **not** be to build the full product. First, run a short smoke-test phase to discover which problem causes real buyer action.
Social engagement is useful as an early signal, but likes and agreeable comments are weak evidence. The evidence ladder should move from engagement → sample request → email/signup → payment → actual use.
### 10–14 day smoke test
Test three different angles that all lead toward the same underlying Product Factory.
#### Angle A — The Weekly Headache
Target community, membership, coaching, and customer-education businesses.
Test whether the recurring obligation itself hurts:
> You run a paid community or membership. Monday comes around again. Now you need something genuinely useful to give members this week — not another AI-generated “5 Tips” post. What takes longer every week: deciding **what** to give them, creating it, or getting members to actually use it?
The goal is to learn whether this is a sufficiently annoying and recurring job.
#### Angle B — The Quiet Supplier
Test the distributor/white-label thesis:
> Instead of selling another marketing tool, what if somebody quietly supplied the finished campaigns and assets your business needs every week? You put your name on it. Your customers get the value. You don't have to create the damn thing. Useful — or solving a problem nobody really has?
This angle can be floated to consultants, agencies, associations, creators, SaaS businesses, and other organizations that already own an audience.
#### Angle C — “This Week Is Handled”
Test the closest version of the actual offer:
> What would it be worth to open one email every Monday morning and think: **Good. This week is handled.** Inside is one useful thing for your customers or members, the posts to introduce it, the email, follow-up, graphic, and everything needed to use it. Not 100 templates. Not a course. One finished weekly campaign.
Use a real call to action such as:
> **Want a sample week? Comment WEEK or send me a DM.**
The key metric is not likes. Track qualified DMs, sample requests, email signups, and eventually purchases.
### Build the MVP backwards from the winning signal
Do not build software, a portal, 52 weeks of material, or a fully automated Product Factory.
The first MVP can be **three finished weekly kits**, created mostly manually.
Choose one audience based on the smoke-test response and build three consecutive editions.
A sample weekly kit could contain:
- One genuinely useful concept
- One polished downloadable asset
- Main teaching/post
- Engagement post or poll
- Follow-up post
- Customer/member email
- Graphic
- 60-second video script
- Simple owner instructions
- White-label version
The goal is not to demonstrate every future feature. The goal is to make the core promise real enough that someone can use it and decide whether it is worth paying for repeatedly.
### Ask for money quickly
After someone receives the sample, offer a simple founding pilot.
Example:
> **Founding Pilot**
> One complete ready-to-use customer/member campaign every week for four weeks.
> **\$29–\$49 for the first month.**
> Limited founding group.
A handful of paying customers is more valuable evidence than a large amount of social engagement.
An illustrative early signal worth continuing might be:
**10+ qualified sample requests → 5+ serious signups/conversations → 3+ paying buyers**
These are learning thresholds, not permanent KPIs. If nobody pays, change the problem, promise, audience, or packaging before investing in more infrastructure.
### Build the Product Factory while fulfilling the MVP
The MVP has a second purpose: begin constructing the internal Product Factory through actual production rather than designing it theoretically.
Use a simple internal pipeline:
**Opportunity → Research → Concept → Asset → Campaign → QA → Package → Deliver**
Run each MVP edition through the existing AI and agent infrastructure and record:
- Human time required
- AI/agent time
- Production cost
- Where quality breaks
- What still requires Jack
- What can be templated
- What can eventually be automated
- What parts are reusable across markets
One particularly important experiment is to take **one core concept** and manufacture several vertical editions, for example:
**Community Coach → Local Business Consultant → SaaS Customer Success**
If roughly 70–80% of the production process can remain common while the final layer creates meaningful niche specificity, the Product Factory starts to have attractive economics.
If every niche requires rebuilding from scratch, that is equally valuable evidence and should change the strategy.
### Suggested 14-day experiment
**Days 1–4:** Publish 6–9 problem/offer posts testing several angles.
**Days 5–6:** Create one simple landing page offering a Sample Week.
**Days 7–9:** Produce one excellent sample kit and deliver it to people who raised their hands.
**Days 10–11:** Offer the four-week founding pilot and ask for payment.
**Days 12–14:** Produce the first paid edition manually through the embryonic Product Factory.
At the end, evaluate behavior rather than opinions:
**Which buyer responded? → Which promise pulled? → Who paid? → What did they actually use? → Can we manufacture it efficiently? → Can somebody else distribute it?**
### Governing principle
Do not improve or automate the factory until there is evidence people want what comes out of it.
The objective of the first trial is therefore twofold:
**Prove demand for the output while learning how to manufacture the output repeatedly.**
That avoids building an impressive machine before proving there is a market for what it produces.
## Second-Layer Insights
These ideas come from stepping back from individual product concepts and combining patterns across the Perfect Product research. They are not recommendations to launch or test a specific business yet. Their purpose is to widen the search space and expose business structures we had not previously put together.
### 1. The Perfect Product may be a Product Ingredient Company
We have repeatedly assumed that ZedBiz needs to own the finished product sold to the end user. That may be the wrong level of the value chain.
Combine the [PLR.me](http://PLR.me) model, the Carex Hip Kit pattern, white-label distribution, channel owners, and the Product Factory concept and a different business appears:
> **ZedBiz manufactures the valuable ingredient that makes somebody else's existing product better.**
The product does not necessarily need to be weekly content. It could be a reusable implementation, engagement, customer-success, decision, or marketing layer that another company bolts onto what it already sells.
Examples of the structure:
- A course company adds a **90-Day Implementation Layer** to its course.
- An association includes a **Member Business Toolkit** with membership.
- A SaaS company gives customers a **Customer Success Pack** that helps them get a result from the software.
- A franchise supplies every franchisee with a **Local Marketing Pack**.
- A directory gives premium advertisers a **Vendor Growth Kit**.
- A consultant includes a **Client Action System** with every engagement.
This changes the sales proposition. We are not asking the buyer to purchase another standalone product. We help them make their **existing product more valuable, useful, sticky, differentiated, or sellable**.
Licensing and white-label economics also become natural because the same underlying intellectual property can be supplied repeatedly to multiple channel owners.
#### Question worth pursuing
> **Which businesses already have customers but have a weak “what happens after they buy?” layer?**
That may be a more interesting hunting ground than asking what consumers need.
### 2. The opportunity may actually be B2B2C — find who loses money when the end user's problem remains unsolved
Across several ideas we keep finding the same structure:
- The **end user experiences the problem**.
- The end user may be a poor customer for ZedBiz.
- A business upstream financially benefits when that end user's problem is solved.
Examples:
**Rural property buyer has uncertainty → realtor or lender benefits from a better-qualified buyer.**
**Community member becomes inactive → community owner loses retention and recurring revenue.**
**Course student gets stuck → course creator suffers poor completion, testimonials, referrals, and repeat sales.**
**Software user fails to implement → SaaS company faces churn.**
**Franchisee struggles with marketing → franchisor suffers weaker locations and brand performance.**
**Association member gets little practical value → association faces weaker renewal.**
**Advertiser does not know how to market → directory or publisher risks advertiser churn.**
This is more than finding a distributor.
The distributor can become **the paying customer** because solving the end user's problem improves the distributor's own economics.
That suggests a new Perfect Product question:
> **Who loses money when the end user's problem isn't solved?**
Instead of only searching for people experiencing pain, look one level upstream for organizations with a financial incentive to solve that pain repeatedly and at scale.
This may reveal markets where the person receiving the value and the person paying for the solution should deliberately be different.
### 3. The Product Factory could create Micro-Brands rather than simply products
The Product Factory idea can be pushed another step.
Instead of ZedBiz becoming one company containing an expanding catalogue of unrelated products, the factory could create **small standalone brands built around one problem**.
Each micro-brand could have:
- One clearly defined problem
- One memorable name
- One flagship product
- One landing site
- One acquisition/distribution mechanism
- Its own customer or partner list
- Recurring or repeat economics where appropriate
- A documented production and operating system
- Minimal founder dependency
Illustrative structures — not current recommendations:
**MemberSpark** — tools community owners give members to create participation.
**AcreageReady** — rural-property decision tools distributed through realtors or lenders.
**ExitReady Digital** — business-sale digital-readiness tools distributed through brokers or accountants.
**CourseFinish** — implementation systems course creators add to courses to improve completion.
**LocalLaunchKit** — campaigns distributed by chambers, directories, agencies, or other local-business channels.
The names and markets are examples only. The important idea is the architecture.
ZedBiz becomes the **holding/manufacturing company** rather than necessarily the consumer-facing brand.
The internal engine becomes:
**Research → identify opportunity → create micro-brand → manufacture IP → establish distribution → systemize → grow, hold, license, sell, or kill.**
This connects directly to the Perfect Product requirement of building a sellable asset.
Instead of eventually trying to sell a complicated ZedBiz containing Jack, client work, experiments, and unrelated projects, a successful micro-brand could potentially be sold independently with its customer base, intellectual property, distribution relationships, revenue, and operating system intact.
The endgame therefore changes from:
> **Build one company with lots of products.**
to:
> **Build a factory capable of creating little companies.**
Some may die quickly. Some may become quiet small cash-flow assets. Occasionally one may become the major business.
## A new combined lens
Putting these three ideas together creates a different way to search for opportunities:
> **Find an end-user problem → identify the company financially hurt by that problem → manufacture a branded solution that company can deploy to its customers → repeat it across many channel owners → spin the successful solution into its own micro-brand.**
That is substantially different from asking:
> **What digital product should Jack sell?**
The more interesting discovery question may now be:
> **What recurring problems affect thousands of end users where somebody upstream has a stronger reason to pay for the solution than the end user does?**
That question deserves to remain open while the Perfect Product research continues.

**Status:** Research screen complete. No product is approved for launch.
## What the evidence eliminates
The market evidence does **not** support a generic digital guide, checklist, prompt pack, or template as Jack’s first product.
### Rural land and acreage buyer guides
There is a genuine, expensive buying moment. Land buyers need to understand access, water, zoning, drainage, septic, utilities, taxes, and financing. That proves pain, not a paid-product opening.
- Major land lenders and marketplaces already give detailed buyer guides away.
- Etsy shows **1,000+ results** for “land buyer guide,” including editable guides and bundles at roughly €5 to €68. Several listings have hundreds or thousands of reviews.
**Decision:** Do not build a direct-to-consumer acreage checklist or generic realtor buyer-guide template.
### Business buyer and seller guides
Buying or selling a business is a serious transaction moment. But BizBuySell, brokers, banks, and business-development centres already give away detailed checklists and seller guides.
- BizBuySell provides free buyer and seller guides, including a detailed digital-asset transfer guide.
- Business-broker vendors sell much broader operating toolkits, including a current \$97 broker toolkit.
**Decision:** Do not sell a general business-buyer, seller-preparation, or digital-asset checklist directly to owners.
### Membership and sponsorship kits
Membership renewal is a real annual pressure point. But association and event software vendors give away renewal templates, checklists, prompts, and sponsorship toolkits as lead-generation material.
**Decision:** Do not build a generic association renewal or sponsorship template bundle.
## The usable insight
The moments are real. The information products are weak because generic information is used as **free lead material** by the companies that already own the customer relationship.
> The possible business is not a generic guide. It is a narrow client-acquisition and decision system sold to the channel owner who already meets the end buyer at the moment of need.
The end buyer receives a useful worksheet, tool, checklist, calculator, or AI-assisted planning path. The actual payer is the broker, lender, adviser, publisher, or similar channel owner who can use it to attract, qualify, or serve their buyers more efficiently.
A plain white-label PDF remains a commodity. A serious system must have a narrow buyer moment, non-generic local or industry detail, lead capture, automatic delivery and follow-up, and a clear way for the channel owner to benefit.
## The two channel-owner hypotheses
### Rural property buyer system
- **End-buyer moment:** A buyer is considering rural or acreage property and needs to decide whether it can support their intended use.
- **Payer:** A rural real-estate agent, land lender, or close partner.
- **Potential value to payer:** More qualified leads and a useful pre-tour or pre-application conversation.
- **Potential product:** A region-specific Rural Property Pre-Offer Reality Check with a lead-capture page, property-visit scorecard, professional-question list, and automatic follow-up copy.
- **Founder fit:** Rural and farming background, commercial-lending view, and local marketing.
- **Red flag:** Generic versions are cheap commodities. Local rules and specialist review are needed. Do not build until a specific channel owner agrees to a fixed, no-customization founding licence.
### Business-sale digital-readiness system
- **End-buyer moment:** An owner is preparing a business for sale and needs digital assets, customer information, operating records, and transition planning organized.
- **Payer:** A business broker, succession adviser, accountant, or lender.
- **Potential value to payer:** Less repeated chasing, a stronger seller intake process, and more organized sale files.
- **Potential product:** A broker-branded Digital Sale File Starter System with a seller workbook, no-password asset inventory, operations and key-person capture prompts, broker intake form, and a non-legal transition checklist.
- **Founder fit:** Marketing, websites, directories, systems, business ownership, and commercial-lending experience.
- **Red flag:** Free seller guides already exist. Do not build until a broker identifies a material gap and agrees to pay for a fixed-scope founding licence.
## What changes now
Jack should not build a guide and then look for buyers.
- Find a channel owner who already has the end buyer at a transaction point.
- Identify a repeated friction in that channel owner’s current process.
- Define one fixed asset that removes the friction.
- Get paid commitment for a no-customization founding licence.
- Only then make the reusable product.
No full product, community, course, marketplace listing, or software build comes before that commitment.
## Strategic fork
### Build a channel-owner product
Build one narrow fixed-licence system only after a channel owner pays a refundable founding deposit. The two possibilities above are only hypotheses.
### Acquire or partner for existing buyer access
If the goal is immediate sales rather than a channel-owner proof cycle, the honest route is not invention. It is acquisition, licensing, or a revenue-share partnership with an existing small product, publication, directory, or marketplace seller that already has customers. That route requires its own financial and operating review.
## Sources
- [BizBuySell: Buyer due diligence checklist](https://www.bizbuysell.com/learning-center/article/due-diligence-checklist-what-to-verify-before-buying-a-business/)
- [BizBuySell: Digital-asset transfer in a business sale](https://www.bizbuysell.com/learning-center/article/transferring-digital-assets-business-sale/)
- [Arkansas Small Business and Technology Development Center: Buyer checklist](https://asbtdc.org/business-buyer-checklist/)
- [Trainual: Broker due diligence guidance](https://trainual.com/manual/mastering-due-diligence-a-guide-for-business-brokers)
- [Become Business Broker: Broker toolkit](https://becomebusinessbroker.com/business-broker-ma-advisor-toolkit/)
- [AgWest: Land buying checklist](https://www.agwestfc.com/financing/country-home-loans/land-loans/land-buying-checklist)

# Mary's Thoughts
*Written by Mary, Sep 28, 2026. The brief Jack gave me: no filters, no evaluations, no re-summarizing what Grok, Manus, or I already covered — three original ideas, formed by connecting dots across everything on the Perfect Product page that nobody's connected yet. These are the three. Status: ideas only, Jack hasn't picked one.*
## Three new angles
### 1. You already bought the Perfect Product.
- The dot nobody connected: the Carex Hip Kit photo. Jack *is* the triggered buyer. He bought a labeled box at the exact moment of need — no webinar, no discovery call, no community, no onboarding sequence. Nobody nurtured him into it. The job landed and the box was sitting there.
- Stop designing for abstract "agency owners." Design for buyers who *are* Jack: blunt, competent, allergic to being sold to. They don't join Skools. They don't watch webinars. They buy the box at midnight.
- That market isn't small — it's every older operator, farmer, tradesperson, and small-town owner in Manus's niche directions. The brand writes itself: "No webinars. No discovery calls. No community. Just the box."
- The product spec becomes a person spec: *would Jack buy this at midnight?* If not, kill it.
### 2. One break, four products.
- The fleet breaks every other day — roughly 180 incidents a year. Right now each break is, at best, one field note.
- Run every incident through the factory *once* and get four products out: the story (the letter), the versioned artifact (the playbook tier), the standalone job kit (Manus's \$29–79 box), and the changelog entry (proof of maintenance).
- "Built once, sold many" applied to *production itself* — the factory is the productized asset, not any single product.
- The kicker nobody's selling: publish the hours. The whole thing visibly runs on about five hours a week. Radical transparency as the anti-guru proof — "the business you can verify runs without the founder." Nobody in this space can show that receipt. Jack can.
### 3. Build the shelf, not the box.
- Everyone — Manus, the GHL-kit page, Mary — has been designing individual kits. But [PLR.me](http://PLR.me) doesn't sell a pack. It sells *18,866* packs to 600,000 buyers. The shelf is the business.
- A tiny, ruthless shelf of one-job kits, labeled by job instead of by guru: "No-show recovery." "Review request engine." "Seasonal promotion." Self-serve, \$29–79 each, no discovery calls, no Jack.
- It starts with Jack's three kits (Manus's homework: three real jobs × six lines each), and every kit added makes the shelf more valuable.
- The shelf itself is the sellable asset — product line, customer list, transaction history — the exact thing a publisher would acquire, by construction.
- First placement: Jack's own directories. The flow he already owns, trait #9, no new audience to grow.
## Three dead concepts — kept as ingredients
*Jack killed all three on Sep 28, 2026. Kept here on his orders: a dead idea plus the right twist plus the perfect ingredient can become a good idea. Don't delete these.*
### 1. Client Retention Engine (dead)
- The idea: monthly white-labeled "Your Marketing This Month" narrative + one client-usable asset per agency client; \~\$5–10/client/mo; agency holds the GHL keys, no trust gate.
- Why Jack killed it: "Client retention is what GHL does. If we're selling to GHL owners and we're selling client retention engine, it's like — oh, you do client retention for your clients? How about we do that for you? ...we're dumb." It sold them their own job.
- Salvageable ingredient: the *question* it was trying to answer — "what am I paying for?" — is real. The error was selling retention-as-a-service instead of selling the agency a *weapon*.
### 2. Award-Submission Factory (dead)
- The idea: fleet turns agency GHL data into polished case studies + award packets, white-labeled, quarterly.
- Why Jack killed it: GHL awards run on GHL's own referral/affiliate data — there are no submissions. "Never heard of it. Can't see it being any value." Mary built on a casual mention instead of verifying. Sloppy.
- Salvageable ingredient: the *factory shape* — fleet turns the agency's raw data into polished proof assets. The error was the fake occasion (awards). The real occasion is the churn moment.
### 3. Wholesale Shelf (dead)
- The idea: 12 seasonal/local campaign kits a year, licensed flat \~\$197–497/mo, deployed across the agency's whole client base.
- Why Jack killed it: "Throw a whole bunch of shit at the wall and hope the GHL people buy it... that's like marketing 110." Generic commodity.
- Salvageable ingredient: the *distribution shape* — one agency sale reaches 50–1,000 end businesses, white-label, agency as distributor. The error was the contents (generic kits), not the channel.
**Standing rule from the kill:** no more framework-first products for a buyer Mary hasn't listened to first. Research owner words before inventing.
## What GHL agency owners actually say (listen-first research, Sep 28, 2026)
*The "HighLevel (GHL) Official Community" Facebook group was login-walled (no saved FB credentials), so fallback was public Reddit: \~9 full threads, 500+ comments across r/gohighlevel and r/agency. Software bug reports and feature requests excluded — business pains only, ranked by frequency.*
1. **Getting clients** (very common): "Cold outreach sucks. We all fucking hate it." The space's meme: buy GHL → fail to get clients → pivot to teaching GHL → students repeat the cycle.
2. **Fulfillment grind** (very common): "Troubleshooting execution logs at 10pm because a client's automation broke." "Broken automations, long nights fixing bugs while a client pings your phone at 2am."
3. **Pricing/packaging** (very common): "What are you actually doing to charge \$2-5k/mo instead of \$297?" Stuck at low SaaS tiers; underpricing because they don't track true per-client cost.
4. **Hiring** (very common): VAs who "couldn't complete basic tasks, even after test runs." Can't tell if a hire knows GHL "or just says they do." White-label fulfillment horror stories — one owner paid \$3,623 across four invoices for a build that arrived still broken after 7 months.
5. **Onboarding/support burden** (common): "I used to spend 2-3 hours on onboarding calls teaching clients the CRM... then they'd forget everything and Slack me to do it for them anyway."
6. **Churn** (common): "I ran traditional retainers for a year. Every month felt like I was re-convincing clients not to churn." And the key line: "Even when results are good, clients still ask 'what am I paying for?'"
7. **Reporting** (occasional, sharp): "Most agencies are doing solid work... but their reporting is messy. A mix of GHL reports, ad screenshots, and spreadsheets. It works, but it doesn't feel valuable to clients... I've seen agencies add a few hundred per client/month just by improving how they present data. GHL alone doesn't really solve this cleanly."
8. **Platform-risk churn** (the surprise): "Meta is actively banning Instagram accounts using native Comment-to-DM workflows. 3 of our accounts nuked this week" → "two of our users have already cancelled their packages... Our agency's revenue and reputation are taking a massive hit because a native GHL feature is treating user assets like sacrificial lambs." Agencies lose clients over platform enforcement they don't control.
9. **What they already pay for:** VAs/freelancers (\$150/mo overseas tech VAs), white-label fulfillment, snapshots, guru courses (\~\$997), prospecting/audit tools, CRM-simplifying Chrome extensions.
Also notable: SaaS-mode psychology — reframing retainer as "buying software, not hiring me" cut one owner's churn from \~25% to under 10%.
## Two new concepts from the research (Sep 28, 2026)
*Jack's brief: don't rebuild the three dead ones. Dig deep, off-the-wall, look broader. Two new concepts, built from the owners' words above. Status: ideas only.*
### 1. The Save Kit — a weapon for the churn moment, not a retention service
- The dot nobody connected: the dead Client Retention Engine + Manus's triggered-kit shape + Jack's own Hip Kit behavior (he buys at the moment of need — no webinar, no nurture). The churn quote is the trigger: "Even when results are good, clients still ask 'what am I paying for?'"
- The twist on the dead idea: don't sell the agency *retention-as-a-service* (their job — insulting). Sell them a *weapon they fire themselves* the moment a client wobbles: one click generates a white-labeled "here's everything we've done for you" proof packet — every automation run, every lead touched, every follow-up sent, every review gained, dollarized where possible — assembled from the agency's own GHL data, not a narrative we write.
- Triggered, not ambient: it fires when the question gets asked or cancellation looms. That's the Hip Kit shape — the labeled box sitting there at the moment of need.
- Why it clears the "don't sell them their job" rule: we're not doing their retention. We're arming it.
- The moat (NotionAI's performance-dataset idea, finally with a home): every save attempt tracked — fired, saved/lost, why. Over time that's a proprietary dataset of what actually stops churn, making every future kit smarter. The dataset is the sellable asset.
- Open validation: does GHL's API expose the workflow-execution and contact-touch data needed to auto-assemble the packet? If yes, buildable; if no, it dies here.
### 2. Platform Weather — early warning for the storms that cancel your clients
- The dot nobody connected: the Meta-nuking quote ("our agency's revenue and reputation are taking a massive hit") + the fleet's daily monitoring habit + the fact that here agencies don't lose clients to competitors — they lose them to *platform weather*.
- The product: monitoring + rapid response. The fleet watches Meta, Google, Twilio, and GHL itself for enforcement waves, policy changes, API deprecations, and breaking changes. When a storm hits, the agency gets (a) early warning before their clients feel it, and (b) pre-written white-labeled client comms — "here's what happened, it's platform-wide, here's our fix, here's what we're doing so it doesn't hit you again."
- The twist: it converts the agency's most humiliating moment (client's account banned, agency looks incompetent) into a heroism moment (agency warned them Tuesday, fix ready Wednesday). It sells *reputation armor*, not information.
- Between storms the monthly value is the brief itself — and GHL's own constant breakage (Jack's fleet breaks every other day on tool churn) means there's always weather.
- Broader than GHL: any business built on rented platforms. Starts with GHL agencies because that's where the quote came from.
- The sellable asset: the wave archive — every enforcement event documented with what broke, who got hit, and which comms worked. Nobody owns this dataset.
